evidence.title: U11: A standard patent takes a median 980 days to grant; a trade mark 223 days to register
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For applications filed FY2010 to FY2019, standard patents took a median 980 days (about 2.7 years) to grant, the middle half 681 to 1,318 days. Trade marks took a median 223 days, with a sharp peak at about 222 days; WIPO gives IP Australia's average time from filing to registration in 2016 as 222 days (U70), so the peak matches the office's usual path.

- 99% of standard patents are granted within 2,156 days; 99% of trade marks within 1,081, with a long tail.
- Designs take a median 33 days and second-tier patents 21; an innovation patent was granted after a check of formalities only, so its 21 days are not compared with standard patents'.
- 57 values remain negative (registered before filed), down from 1,497 before the repairs. They are left as recorded.

evidence.title: Lens: IP rights
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
1. Where a right's applicants have no country recorded, its origin is "unknown", not "overseas". Why: Counting the unknowns as overseas had added 517,145 old patents to the overseas side.
2. Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents. Why: They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.
3. Two placeholder dates are emptied (an end date of 1 January 1970 on 1,282 rights, and one registration before the register began). Why: 1 January 1970 is the "zero" of computer dates, standing in for an unknown date, not a real one.
4. Trade marks registered before 1986 have no "days to registration". Why: The register holds only their filing date, so their recorded time to registration is almost always zero.
5. The "technology area" is kept for patents only. Why: For every trade mark and design it simply repeated the class of goods, so it measured nothing new.

evidence.title: U31: Each right's milestones were added only after five checks of how the register records them
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Eleven columns of milestones (examination, acceptance, opposition, assignment, extension, lifetime) rest on five checks of IP RAPID's event records. Among them: trade marks' recorded ends fall from 3,213 in March 2026 to 0 from May, probably because an end is recorded only after the grace period for renewal, so trade marks and designs are treated as observed only to 31 March 2026.

- **No separate grant column.** A patent's grant event falls on its registration date for 99.99% of granted patents.
- **Assignments counted once.** 99.78% of patents with an assignment have it published twice, as an assignment and as a party change; the first is used.
- **Only standing events.** 4.76% of patent lapse events were later reversed, and 60.47% of the patents with one are now granted, expired or ceased.
- **When a term starts.** 92.19% of ceased trade marks whose two filing dates differ (mostly international ones) end a whole number of years after the earliest; 84.59% of standard patents ceased since 1996 end 6 to 7 months after an anniversary, at the end of the grace period.

evidence.title: U70: The United States files about four in ten patent applications at IP Australia; China now files as many as Australians
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Of patent applications at IP Australia, the United States filed 41.2% in 1995, 45.6% in 2004 and 41.9% in 2024. Australians filed 12.7%, 11.2% and 8.3%; China 0.0%, 0.3% and 8.3%. Three-quarters of Australians' own applications (76.1% in 2024) are made abroad.

- IP Australia beside other OECD offices (2024): 405 patent examiners (median office 83.5); 347 days from an examination request to the first action (median 210); trade marks 37 days to the first action (median 30).
- WIPO gives IP Australia's average time to register a trade mark as 222 days (2016), the peak found in IP RAPID (U11). So the peak is consistent with the office's usual path to registration; WIPO's figure is an average, and IP RAPID's mean for FY2010 to FY2019 is 286.5 days.
- Australian residents' applications at every office were 4,389 (1995), 10,631 (2005) and 10,633 (2024), against 1,784, 2,555 and 2,542 at IP Australia.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The median time from a standard patent's examination request to its acceptance rose from 408 days (FY1990) to 755 (FY2006), and has been 422 to 516 days since FY2014. Trade marks went from 666 days to acceptance (FY1990) to 52 to 184 days from FY2005.

- Filing to examination request, standard patents: 192 days (FY2000), 652 (FY2005), 552 (FY2010), 309 (FY2015) and 553 (FY2021). For FY2013 it is 44 days: applicants asked for examination before Raising the Bar took effect, which kept their applications under the old law.
- Certification: 123 to 208 days after grant for innovation patents and 73 to 276 days after registration for designs.
- The latest years are still in progress, so their medians are understated.

evidence.title: B2: The strongest pairs are how the IP system works, not findings, and are recorded but not carried forward
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The strongest leads are what the filing rules and the way records are made would produce anyway. Australian filers file their international (PCT) applications at IP Australia (strength 0.945), and the inventions they file are made here (0.892). A patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination (0.83).

- Each held in the earlier decade too: 0.938, 0.851 and 0.817.
- **The applicant sets part of the pace.** A standard patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination; the office is not the only source of delay.
- **A record effect.** Wider families have fewer inventors of unknown country (0.526; 0.582), because Google Patents takes inventors' countries from foreign publications, which narrow families lack (U95).
- **Trade marks:** expedited examination goes with a priority claim (0.78; 0.763), the recording U103 explained.
- **Provisionals:** individuals have no ABN (0.757; 0.738). **Trade marks:** a founding applicant's country goes with its priority office (0.731; 0.774).

evidence.title: U27: Patent grants peaked in 2016; trade mark cessations reached their highest in 2025
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Patent grants peaked at 25,687 in 2016, three years after the rush to file before Raising the Bar, and were 19,612 in 2025. Trade mark registrations reached 70,634 in 2021. Trade mark cessations (registered marks let go) rose from 7,240 in 1996 to 35,484 in 2025, the peak, though not steadily: 29,802 in 2019 and 28,319 in 2023.

- Patent expiries rose from 30 (1996) to 4,019 (2025), as patents filed under the 20-year term reach it.
- Ownership transfers: trade mark assignments peaked at 18,370 (2019), patent assignments at 6,015 (2015).
- Trade mark oppositions rose from 824 (1996) to 2,309 (2025, the peak).
- Trade mark cessations fell to 3,773 in 2002 while lapses rose: accounted for by the gap between two Acts' first terms and the large filing year of 2000 (U38).

pool.text:
- **Later standard patents more often stay in force; about half of trade marks are still in force after ten years.** Standard patents' median time in force rose from 10.6 years (granted in the 1980s and 1990s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). These are shares still on the register, not value; the research owner adopted years in force as a working measure for Stage 2, alongside other signals. Observations: U36.
- **US patents often cite Australian research, and R&D spending has fallen.** US patents often cite Australian research institutions' work; 93.6% of those citations come from patents with no Australian applicant or inventor, as most US patents have none. - **The register's history shapes what it can say.** Early years hold only the rights that survived until records were computerised; some events were dated in batches; patent ownership history starts in FY2003. Each is handled, but each limits comparisons over time. Observations: U23, U17, U34.

pool.title: U36: Later standard patents are more often still in force at 10 and 15 years; about half of trade marks are still in force after ten years
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For each granted or registered right, take its years in force from grant or registration, and whether it has ended.
2. Group rights into cohorts by the date their term follows.
3. For each cohort, work out the share still in force after each number of years, counting unfinished rights for as long as they have run (a Kaplan–Meier survival curve); readings with fewer than 30 rights still at risk are left blank.
4. Read off the median and the shares in force after 10 and 15 years. A patent ends on the record six months after the anniversary at which it was not renewed, so "after 10 years" means after the ninth anniversary's renewal; a trade mark ends at the anniversary, so "after 10 years" means after the tenth anniversary's renewal fell due.

**Which gives observation U36:** Of standard patents granted in the 1980s, 53.2% were still in force 10 years after their date of patent; of those from the 2000s and 2010s, 67.5% and 67.3%. The median time in force rose from 10.6 years (1980s and 1990s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). For trade marks the share still in force after 10 years fell, from 67.0% of those filed 1983 to 1989 to 46.9% of the 2000s' and 47.5% of the 2010s'.

pool.title: B25: Within firms, the first trade mark usually comes before the first patent or design; one first filing in five is dated before the firm's first public registration
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Of 4,550 firms with a first trade mark and a first standard patent both filed FY2010 to FY2026, 72.86% filed the trade mark first; of 3,851 with a first trade mark and a first design, 65.62%. Measured from the firm's first public registration, first trade marks came a median 2.61 years after it and first standard patents 5.22 years. But 18.02% of first trade marks and 19.57% of first standard patents are dated before that registration.

- **Trade marks:** 32.25% of first trade marks came within the firm's first year, and 17.99% after 10 years or more. **Standard patents:** 7.11% within the first year, 29.65% after 10 years or more. **Designs:** a median 5.24 years.
- **Firms first seen from 2001 only:** 2.24 years for trade marks, 3.97 for standard patents and 3.96 for designs; shorter, since such a firm can be at most about 25 years old here.
- **One in five before registration.** For those firms the registration date is not the business's start, so a recorded age is not a lower bound on age at filing for about one firm in five.

pool.title: U109: In real terms a trade mark costs about a quarter of what it did in 1990, and keeping a patent for its full term costs what it did in 1995
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
In dollars of June 2026, a trade mark (one class, filing and registration) cost 944 in January 1990 and 250 now. A standard patent's filing, examination and grant fell from 2,261 (January 1995) to 1,250. Its renewals for the full term cost 16,140 in January 1995, 11,992 in January 2010 and 16,550 now.

- **Designs:** 0.4% and 0.7% never registered in the second half of 1985, then 26.3% in the first quarter of 1986.
- The survivor months had counted 44,231 trade marks from Australian applicants and 75,470 from overseas ones (3.1% and 8.5% of each series).
- **Batches.** Patent cessations were dated in batches to April 1995: 29.8% of the 104 months from September 1986 hold none.
- **Partial records.** Grants are recorded only for patents filed from 1979: 1.0% to 1.9% of standard patents filed in 1976 to 1978 have a grant date, against 68.5% of those filed in 1979.

pool.title: U25: Growth in standard patents has slowed to 0.4% a year; trade marks and designs are growing faster
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Standard patent applications grew 3.9% a year in the 1990s, 1.3% from 2000 to 2010, 2.0% from 2010 to 2019 and 0.4% from 2019 to 2025, with overseas applicants setting the pace. Trade marks grew 4.3% a year and designs 5.5% a year from 2019 to 2025.

- Australians' standard patents grew 1.1%, 2.5%, 0.9% and 0.9% a year in the four periods (by the filer's origin); overseas applicants' 4.2%, 1.1%, 2.1% and 0.3%.
- Trade marks grew 6.9%, 3.3%, 2.7% and 4.3% a year in the four periods, so their growth since 2019 is faster than in the 2010s but slower than in the 1990s.
- Designs grew almost entirely from overseas; Australians' ran at 1,903 (2022) to 2,678 (2013) a year from 1990.
- **Falls.** In 2009, standard patents fell 10.9% (26,598 to 23,707), designs 15.2% and trade marks 4.5%, the year after the global financial crisis began; trade marks fell 11.2% in 2022 from the 2021 peak.

pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the IP rights lens)
pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. Every trade mark and design was read from IP Australia's register through its APIs on 27 October 2026.
   - _Why:_ A sample can check accuracy, but filling gaps needs every record, so that every year is filled alike.
2. A filled value keeps IP RAPID's and takes the register's only where IP RAPID has none.
   - _Why:_ IP RAPID stays the base, and its own values can always be compared with the filled ones.

**Repairs made to the IP rights lens before any observation**

1. Where a right's applicants have no country recorded, its origin is "unknown", not "overseas".
   - _Why:_ Counting the unknowns as overseas had added 517,145 old patents to the overseas side.
2. Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
   - _Why:_ They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.

A standard patent typically takes much longer: **U11 (descriptive)** found a median **980 days** from filing to grant for applications filed **FY2010 to FY2019**, compared with **223 days** from filing to registration for a trade mark. [1]

The median is the middle wait—not a guaranteed processing time. For standard patents, the middle half took **681 to 1,318 days**, so there was considerable variation. [2]

Two qualifications help interpret the comparison:
- **These are successful applications.** U12 (descriptive), which tracks waits by filing year, counts only applications that were later registered or granted. [3]
- **The patent wait is not all office processing time.** B2 (descriptive) found that time to grant goes together with how long applicants wait before requesting examination; the office is not the only source of delay. [4]

evidence.text:
Divisional applications rose from 11.59% to 22.62% of Australian organisations' standard patents between FY2000 to FY2009 and FY2010 to FY2019, and from 7.08% to 15.63% of overseas organisations'. With the field, co-filers and classes held the rise holds (+10.7 and +8.8 points), it holds without the ten filers with the most divisionals, and it holds within the same filers: +19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones.

- **Australian organisations:** +11.0 raw, +10.7 held together (96.9% left). Without the ten filers with the most later divisionals, +7.1.
- **Overseas organisations:** +8.5 raw, +8.8 held together; without their ten largest +8.4. Their ten largest hold 8.51% of the later divisionals.
- So Stage 2's doubling is not a change in the mix of fields or filers: the same organisations file more divisionals.
- Why is not in the data. Stage 2's lead, that a divisional keeps claims pending longer, needs the dates of each divisional's parent and its examination.

evidence.text:
Things the analysis has found but cannot yet explain. They are kept in view, not explained away. Several are closed or narrowed: IP RAPID's innovation patents in 2016 (U67), by the review against IP Australia; the trade mark expedite fall of November 2018 (U34), by IP Australia's own register (U103); most of the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (B11), by a gap in older records (B55); and about half of the recent fall in first patent filers, by the name match (M12).

- Australians' direct filing of standard patents rose to 28.3% in FY2026 (U90), and provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed up less often, mostly by new and heavy individual filers (B38, M35); both could be priority claims recorded late (OQ18).
- The share of divisional applications about doubled among both Australian and overseas organisations, within the same filers (B15, M26); why is not in the data.
- Firms with a first observed patent fell from 1,167 (FY2021) to 810 (FY2024); innovation patents closed in August 2021 (U45). About half of the later fall is linking (M12).

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Asking for examination sooner is not a sign of a longer life.** Expedited examination's link with staying in force does not survive the filer, field and route held together, and Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year. On the wider measure IP Australia's commissioned study uses, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383), against the study's finding. Observations: M5, M40.
- **Some Australian invention ends up owned overseas, by two routes.** Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type, and so are patents filed before the firm's first registration. Inventions made here and filed from overseas come in about equal numbers from international teams and from all-Australian ones. Observations: M6, M27, M30.
- **The same organisations file more divisionals.** Divisionals doubled within the same filers (+19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones), not through a change in fields or filers. Observations: M26.

pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. One row per ANZSIC division and financial year, FY1990 to FY2026.

1. Each right is split over industries by probabilities (an "expected count"), so a division's count is a sum of shares.

pool.text:

No—the atlas finds that the rise in divisional applications was **not explained by a change in technology fields or in who was filing**. Stage 3’s **M26 (observational)** found that the rise held within the same organisations, as well as with technology field, co-filers and number of classes held together. [1]

A divisional is a new application split off from an earlier one, keeping its date; it often protects a different part of the same invention. [2]

### What changed?
The earlier **B15 (descriptive)** finding that divisionals roughly doubled was tested again in M26, with the outcome **holds**. [3] Among organisations’ standard patents, the divisional share rose between FY2000 to FY2009 and FY2010 to FY2019:
- **Australian organisations:** from **11.59% to 22.62%**. [4]
- **Overseas organisations:** from **7.08% to 15.63%**. [4]

### What did the further checks show?
M26 found that the rise remained with technology field, co-filers and number of classes held together, and after excluding the ten filers with the most divisionals. [5] Looking within the same filers, the rise was **+19.18 points for Australian organisations** and **+10.97 for overseas ones**—supporting the reading that the same organisations were filing more divisionals, rather than the overall mix shifting towards different filers. [1]

**What remains unknown is why those organisations changed their filing behaviour.** M26 says that is not in the data; investigating whether divisionals keep claims pending longer needs the dates of each divisional’s parent application and its examination. [6] These are observational checks, not a causal explanation: factors not held together could still matter.

pool.text:
- **Batches.** Patent cessations were dated in batches to April 1995: 29.8% of the 104 months from September 1986 hold none, and others hold several months' worth (46,671 cessations, 11% of the series). Expiries to December 1994 hold 29.4% of their series. Both are dated weekly or daily since (the chart).
- **Partial records.** IP RAPID records grants only for patents filed from 1979: 1.0% to 1.9% of standard patents filed in 1976 to 1978 have a grant date, against 68.5% of those filed in 1979. So the 16,557 grants before 1985 are some of the grants made (2.5% of the series).
- **What remains real.** Patent expiries all but stop from July 1995 and resume in July 1999 (the chart; measured in 5.4). Australia raised the standard patent term from 16 to 20 years on 1 July 1995, for every patent still in force, so patents filed from July 1979 expired four years later than they would have. The policy register now holds this change, checked against the Act (the Patents (World Trade Organization Amendments) Act 1994), and its note on the Patents Act 1990, which said the 1990 Act brought in 20-year patents, is corrected: the 1990 Act's term was 16 years.

evidence.title: M25: Raising the Bar's rush, and Australians' lower level of patents after it, hold with trend and season held; the Designs Act's step does not stand apart
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Read as an interrupted time series with each series' trend and season held, Raising the Bar (April 2013) brought a rush of Australians' standard patents (0.605 in logs) and a lower level after it (a step of -0.334, about 28% fewer a month), which then recovers; its controls were quiet but for one small series. The Designs Act 2003's step for overseas applicants (June 2004) does not stand apart: Australians' trade marks, a control, stepped too.

- **Raising the Bar:** a slope of +0.089 a year after the step, a lower level that then recovers. **Overseas applicants:** a rush of 0.352, no step detected (-0.047).
- **Its controls:** Australians' designs, rush 0.049 and step -0.077, quiet; plant breeder's rights, rush 0.206, a small and noisy series. Stage 2's reading holds, with the plant breeder's rights' rush as a caution.
- **The Designs Act 2003:** overseas applicants' designs step 0.391; but Australians' designs step too (0.162), and so do Australians' trade marks (0.251), while Australians' standard patents do not (0.036).

evidence.title: U28: Around some policy changes filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses; around others nothing stands out
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
In April 2013, the month Raising the Bar took effect, Australians filed 1,044 standard patent applications, 4.41 times their average month in the year before. In August 2021, when the innovation patent closed to new applications, 2,789 second-tier applications came in (4.31 times), then 95.9% fewer a month in the year after. Patent expiries fell 98.4% when the term rose to 20 years.

- **Rushes before a change:** Raising the Bar (Australians 4.41 times their usual month, overseas applicants 2.65 times; in the year after, 34.0% and 7.7% fewer a month) and the innovation patent's closure. Filing also rose after each change was enacted and before it took effect: second-tier applications by 176.4%, Australian standard patents by 45.3%.
- **Steps:** patent expiries (the 20-year term), extensions of term (the 1999 scheme, from 0.08 to 11.17 a month), second-tier applications when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent (+71.5%), and designs under the Designs Act 2003 (overseas applications +40.4%, Australians' +3.4%).

evidence.title: B37: Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month; most of those breaks were certain by law, and few show applicants' behaviour
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For each policy change, the size of the jump or step in the series it targets was compared with the same measure at up to 72 placebo months, five years either side. Seven of the eight changes moved at least one target series further than any placebo month; the Patents Act 1990 did not. Most of these breaks were made certain by the law or the office's processing (no expiries under a longer term, no applications once a right closed). Those that show applicants' behaviour are the rush before Raising the Bar and, perhaps, overseas applicants' step under the Designs Act 2003.

- **Behaviour: Raising the Bar (April 2013).** Australians' and overseas applicants' standard patents both jumped further than in any of 72 placebo months, and Australians' filing stayed lower in the year after. Series it should not have moved (Australians' designs, plant breeder's rights) did not: 37.5% to 81.94% of placebo months moved as much.
- **Behaviour or administration: the Designs Act 2003 (June 2004).** Overseas applicants' designs stepped up further than in any placebo month; Australians' designs did not step beyond the ordinary (61.11% of placebo months as large).

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Across countries and industries, patents follow business R&D.** Across OECD members, patenting at home follows business R&D at the same income and size; across industries, patents allocated per business follow business R&D at the same value added. Australia is nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden on non-IP indicators. Observations: M17, M18, M22.
- **Institutions: research that patents cite goes with their own patenting; licence income does not follow patents.** Across every kind of institution, with kind and size held, research that patents cite goes with more patents per work. At the same research spend, more patents are not seen to go with more licence income. Observations: M38, M24.
- **Raising the Bar's rush holds; the business cycle barely shows.** With trend and season held, Raising the Bar's rush and Australians' lower level of patents after it hold, while the Designs Act's step does not stand apart from a control. With block resampling, the cycle shows only in overseas applicants' trade marks before 2008. Trade marks share a long-run path with real GDP and run a quarter ahead of it, as IP Australia's note finds, but the lead is small once GDP's own growth is held and is not detected since 2008. Observations: M25, M36, M19, M39.

FY2025 and FY2026 are not lower than earlier years for standard patents (29,950 and 31,136, against 28,798 to 32,960 in FY2017 to FY2024), trade marks (92,470 and 98,189) or designs (10,126 and 10,388, the decade's highest). section: How this moves the research forward
pool.text:
Stage 3 answers none of the five questions either: it tests which of Stage 2's signals survive with their other factors held together. This is how the result prepares the ground for them.

- **Q1. What public value does the IP system create?** Patents filed before the firm existed on the register are the ones more often held only overseas now, which bears on where value from early-stage invention goes (the fourth early signal).
- **Q2. Who benefits, and who is underserved?** Points to founders or pre-registration businesses as a group whose patents more often end up overseas.

_Linking an observation to a question is the analyst's guide to where it may help. It is not a finding._

events.answer:
**The evidence strongly supports a rush associated with Raising the Bar, but it does not establish causation.** Stage 3’s M25 (observational) found that the rush remained visible after allowing for the usual trend and seasonal pattern in filings.[1]

Raising the Bar tightened Australia’s patent law from **15 April 2013**; applicants rushed to file and request examination under the old rules.[2]

### What makes the evidence persuasive?

- **A clear spike:** U28 (descriptive) found that Australians filed **1,044 standard patent applications in April 2013**, **4.41 times** their average month in the year before.[3]
- **Unusual timing, not just an ordinary fluctuation:** B37 (observational) found that Australian and overseas standard patent filings both jumped further around the reforms than in any of **72 placebo months**—comparison months used to check how unusual the movement was.[4]
- **The signal survives a stronger check:** M25 (observational) examined the interruption around the reforms while holding each series’ trend and season together. It found a rush for both Australian and overseas applicants, followed by a lower level for Australians—**about 28% fewer a month**—that then recovered; no post-reform step was detected for overseas applicants.[5]
- **Comparison series mostly support the reading:** In M25, Australians’ design filings were quiet around the change. Plant breeder’s rights showed a rush too, however, which the atlas flags as a caution because that series is small and noisy.[6]

### How far can we take that?

Taken together, these findings support the interpretation that applicants brought filings forward around the rule change, rather than the spike being an ordinary monthly fluctuation.[7] But M25 remains **observational**, and the comparison-series caution matters.[8] Allowing for trend and season is not the same as an experiment: other factors not included in the analysis could still help explain the pattern.

So the careful answer is: **a behavioural rush is well supported; a definitive causal claim is not.**[9]

B37's reading (a behavioural rush, controls quiet) **holds** for Australians' standard patents with trend and season held, with the plant breeder's rights' rush as a caution.

Applied, it closes most of the recent fall in patents linked to an ABN and changes no firm finding. Adopting it is the owner's decision (OQ26). Observations: M12, U126.

evidence.title: M12: A name match to the business register recovers most missing business numbers accurately, and changes no firm finding
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the firms lens)
evidence.text:
**For this observation**

1. The filer's name is matched to the ABR's main names and ASIC's company names (current and former), and a match is kept only if exactly one ABN has the name and is registered in the filer's state (name_matched_abn, ADR 0045 and 0047).
   - _Why:_ A name shared by several ABNs, or found in another state, is too likely to be the wrong firm.
2. The match is tested on rights whose ABN is known, with the ABN hidden.
   - _Why:_ Shows how often the match is right before it is used where the ABN is missing.

**Repairs made to the firms lens before any observation**

1. Applications are credited to the business that filed them, not the one that holds them now.
   - _Why:_ Otherwise a firm's filing record would change whenever it bought or sold rights.
2. The ABNs that only IPLORD links to IP are flagged, and IPLORD's own counts are kept out.
   - _Why:_ IPLORD counts differently from IP RAPID; adding the two would mix measures.

evidence.title: Glossary: Name match (to the business register)
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: **Name match (to the business register).** An ABN found for an Australian organisation's right that has none, by matching the filer's name to the ABR's main names and ASIC's company names, kept only if exactly one ABN has the name in the filer's state. Tested on rights with a known ABN; kept apart from the counts, never added to them (ADR 0045, 0047).

evidence.title: M12: A name match to the business register recovers most missing business numbers accurately, and changes no firm finding
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Matching Australian organisations' rights that have no filer's ABN to the ABR's and ASIC's names recovers a known ABN for 66% to 85% of rights where the ABN was hidden for a test, with 1.1% to 4.8% of matches naming another ABN. Applied to rights with no ABN it links 17.7% to 35.3% of them. It closes most of the recent fall in standard patents linked to an ABN, and moves concentration and the claimants' figures by less than a point.

- **The test:** standard patents FY2010 to FY2019, 83.41% matched and 81.70% recovered; FY2020 to FY2026, 68.95%, 67.85% and 1.60% another ABN. Trade marks 78.89%, 76.59% and 2.91%. Designs filed FY2000 to FY2009 are the weakest, 9.84% another ABN. A "wrong" ABN can be a related company of the same group.
- **With the postcode as well**, 42.62% to 46.04% matched, with 2.34% to 4.71% another ABN: it halves the matches for no gain in accuracy, so it was dropped.

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (1 step for this observation, on the research institutions lens)
evidence.text:
**For this observation**

1. An institution's rights are those where it is among the filers, matched by a reviewed list of names (including former names and companies) and business numbers.
   - _Why:_ Universities file under many names; a name decides, and a business number matches only where the name does not (ADR 0021).

**Repairs made to the research institutions lens before any observation**

1. Institutions are linked to rights, grants and contracts through a reviewed list of 116 extra names and 146 ABNs.
   - _Why:_ Universities file under former names, predecessors' names and their commercialisation companies' names.
2. An institution's works and citations are its own, never added across institutions or from a child to its parent.
   - _Why:_ A paper with authors at two institutions counts for both.

evidence.title: U126: The name match's columns are set only where they should be, and add 2% to 8% to the counts by ABN, concentrated in a few firms
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (2 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Check the column is set only for Australian organisations' rights with no filer's ABN.
2. Count what it adds, by kind of right and by firm.

**Which gives observation U126:** The name match finds an ABN for 16.48% of Australian organisations' trade marks with no filer's ABN, and 28.95% of standard patents, but none of the plant breeder's rights. Counted by firm, the matched filings add 2.03% to the standard patents credited by ABN, 2.80% to trade marks and 7.59% to provisionals, concentrated in a few large organisations. They are kept apart, never added to the counts.

evidence.title: Limits and assumptions
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The binding limit on what this research can say is how well its datasets link together. These are the links the two stages found weakest.

- **Firms.** Firms reach IP only through business numbers on applications, so firms' IP counts are lower bounds; IP RAPID's recent filings carry fewer, and IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs (U41, U45, U100). A name match recovers most of the rest and changes no firm finding, but is kept apart from the counts (M12). Size and industry reach only employers of 100 or more (U112), the main third factor every firm signal lacks.

evidence.text:
**For this observation**

1. Firms are placed by their business register postcode. "No filing linked" means no application is linked to the claimant's ABN by IP RAPID's filer's ABN or IP Australia's register (ADR 0036); "no link to IP" means also no right held, no other IP record and no IPLORD link.

**Repairs made to the places lens before any observation**

1. Applications are counted at the filer's postcode, not the current holder's.
   - _Why:_ A right sold to a firm elsewhere should stay where it was filed.
2. A rate is shown only where 10 or more applications would be expected at the national rate.
   - _Why:_ A count of 10 has a 95% range of about 5 to 18 by chance alone; below that, an area's rate is mostly noise.
3. Small areas can be pooled into 335 larger ones (SA3s).
   - _Why:_ So that every area's filings count somewhere, even where its own rate is too uncertain to show.

evidence.title: U101: More firms had their first observed trade mark in FY2026; most had no earlier link to IP
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
A firm's first observed filing is its earliest application linked to its business number, not necessarily its first ever. Counted by IP RAPID's business numbers, firms with a first observed trade mark fell from 11,318 in FY2024 to 7,384 in FY2026. With the register's numbers filled in, they rose: 14,728 in FY2024, 15,818 in FY2025 and 19,730 in FY2026.

- First designs: 414 against 535 filled (FY2024), 342 against 608 (FY2026).
- **Some are not new.** 2.45% to 5.76% of each year's first observed filers already had an earlier trade mark on another record (483 of 19,730 in FY2026), and 4.32% to 9.1% had some earlier link to IP (852 in FY2026). The counts overstate new filers by about that much.
- **And some are missed.** A firm whose first filing carries no business number anywhere is missed, or counted in a later year. So the counts are neither upper nor lower bounds on new filers: both errors are present.

pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. Each firm is placed by the postcode of its main business address in the business register, then given that postcode's remoteness and advantage (IRSAD tenth) from the ABS.

1. Applications are credited to the business that filed them, not the one that holds them now.

2. The ABNs that only IPLORD links to IP are flagged, and IPLORD's own counts are kept out.
   - _Why:_ IPLORD counts differently from IP RAPID; adding the two would mix measures.

pool.title: Limits and assumptions
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
- Public data are taken to be what their publishers say they are. Where checks found otherwise (placeholder dates, mislabelled countries, numbers counted twice), the data were repaired and the repair recorded; elsewhere, the publisher's values stand.
- A business is identified by its ABN. Related companies in a group have different ABNs and are counted apart.
- A place is a postal area, reached through the postcode recorded on an application or in the business register. A registered address may be a head office or an adviser's, not where the work is done.
- An industry is reached through what a right protects (its technology or goods classes), by published probabilities, because few firms in the corpus have an industry.
- Gender is estimated from first names and countries, as a probability summed over many people; it says nothing about any one person, and is read only for inventors in Australia.
- Money is shown as recorded (nominal) unless a page says otherwise; fees are also shown in June 2026 dollars, adjusted with the quarterly Consumer Price Index.
- Where a series begins with only the survivors of an earlier system, or with partial records, those years are left out rather than estimated.

pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Of 17,627 active R&D Tax Incentive claimants placed in a postal area, 48.3% have no IP filing linked to their business number, and 44.7% have no link to IP of any kind. events.answer:
**Yes—matching firm names can recover missing Australian Business Numbers (ABNs), but it does not recover them all and some matches identify a different business number.** Stage 3’s **M12**, a descriptive finding, found that the method closes most of the recent fall in standard patents linked to an ABN without materially changing the firm-level findings. [1]

### How the matching works
M12 matches the filer’s name against business-register main names and current and former company names. It keeps a match only when exactly one ABN has that name and is registered in the filer’s state; names shared by several ABNs, or found in another state, are rejected. [2]

To test accuracy, the researchers hid the ABN on rights where it was already known, then checked whether the name match recovered it. This tests the method against a known answer before applying it to missing records. [3]

### How well does it work?
M12’s descriptive results distinguish between success in the test and success on genuinely missing records:

- **With the known ABN hidden:** the method recovered the known number for **66% to 85%** of rights, with **1.1% to 4.8%** of matches naming another ABN. [4]
- **Applied where the ABN was missing:** it linked **17.7% to 35.3%** of those rights. So useful recovery is possible, but many records remain unlinked. [5]
- **Accuracy varies:** designs filed **FY2000 to FY2009** were the weakest case, with **9.84%** of matches naming another ABN; a different ABN can also belong to a related company in the same group. [6]

Adding postcode to the matching rule was tried but dropped: it halved the matches without improving accuracy. [7]

### What difference does it make to the findings?
For the descriptive observation **U45**, M12’s refinement shows that the apparent recent fall in patent linkage is mostly a recording issue. With name-matched links, the share of standard patents linked to an ABN goes from **89.43% (FY2024) to 89.20% (FY2026)**, compared with **88.68% to 83.85%** using the filer’s recorded ABN. [8]

The broader results are stable: M12 reports that adding the matched links for comparison moves concentration and the claimants’ figures by less than a point. [9]

### What remains unresolved?
**The matched numbers are currently kept beside the main counts, not added to them.** Whether to adopt them into the firms’ counts is an open decision for the research owner. [10]

The method also uses only main business names and company names—not trading and business names, which the atlas identifies as a remaining data gap. [11] Taken together, the evidence supports name matching as a useful repair and a check on whether missing links distort findings, rather than a complete replacement for recorded ABNs. [1]

evidence.title: B29: Filing rises steeply with advantage and falls with remoteness; both hold when read together, in both halves of the areas
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For each standard deviation of advantage (the IRSAD score), a postal area files 1.717 times as many standard patents per person (1.857 in the second half; 1.884 with areas pooled into larger SA3s). Inner regional areas file at 0.259 of major cities' rate. Read together, advantage's ratio is 1.442 and inner regional areas still file at 0.382 of the cities' rate at the same advantage (that combined reading was not repeated for SA3s).

- Trade marks 1.648 (1.707; 1.477), designs 1.504, provisionals 1.582. Very remote areas file standard patents at 0.173 of the cities' rate.
- **The shape is not a straight line:** standard patents run 0.33 to 0.75 a year per 10,000 people across deciles 1 to 8, then 1.51 to 1.62 in deciles 9 and 10. Most of the gradient is in the most advantaged fifth of areas; trade marks rise more steadily (7.63 to 29.24).
- The top tenth differs most between the halves (1.62 against 3.37 for standard patents) because its five heaviest filing areas, several of them mostly one firm's patents (U52), fall in the second half. Pooled rates there are fragile; the overall ratio is the steadier reading.

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries; the signals of value disagree.** Filed in the same number of countries, Australian organisations' patents more often stay in force for 10 years than overseas organisations', except those filed only in Australia. But they reach fewer countries and are cited less, mostly because of that reach. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete in the records, so these are read from FY2010. Observations: B8, B11, B12, B55.
- **Filing follows advantage and remoteness, not one firm.** Each step of area advantage goes with 1.7 to 1.9 times the standard patent rate, and the gradient holds with remoteness allowed for and with each area's largest filer taken out. Areas that gained graduates or income over a decade were not seen to gain filing, so it looks like a standing difference between places. Observations: B29, B30, B58, B59.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Besides testing signals, Stage 3 asked which measures repeat each other and whether there are distinct kinds of place or country. These are descriptive.

- **Places' characteristics are mostly one advantage gradient.** Across 2,525 postal areas the first component, advantage, carries 49.5% of the variation, and IRSAD can be predicted almost entirely from the other measures. No single measure (income, education) should be read as the one that matters. Observations: M13.
- **Places form a continuum, not kinds.** The best grouping of areas has a silhouette of 0.269, short of clear segments; one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas holds 56% of the placed standard patents. Observations: M16.
- **Countries differ along several dimensions.** Across 35 OECD members the first component carries 24.7% of the variation. Australia is low on manufacturing and exports, high on education and new businesses, and nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden. Observations: M17.
- **Trends dominate the monthly series.** Trade marks' and overseas applicants' series are almost all trend; seasons are strong for provisionals and Australians' trade marks; what is left of different series moves together only moderately, perhaps the calendar. Observations: M20.

evidence.text: - **Stage 2, pairs of variables.** When: Complete (28 October 2026; reviewed 2 November) Asks: Which pairs of measures move together, in what shape, how strongly, and for whom? How: Within each lens, every pair of variables was screened on one scale. A pair counted as a lead only if it was at least small, survived the correction for the number of pairs tested, and held in a second period or sample; the planned pairs were then measured in plain units, with intervals. Example: Postal areas with more advantaged residents file 1.7 to 1.9 times as many standard patents per person for each step of advantage, and the gradient is not one firm's (B29, B30). Adds: The first **observational** evidence: associations that bear on who benefits (Q2) and on the conditions for value (Q3), each with its candidate third factors. Done when: Every pair within each lens screened; each lead with its size and interval, past the correction and held in a second sample.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
- **713 areas** (11,871,712 residents, the most), above average on advantage (0.78): 0.59 patents and 13.37 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
- The other three groups (260, 539 and 725 areas) are below average on advantage (-0.80, -0.30 and -0.80), file 0.37 to 0.48 patents and 8.76 to 10.63 trade marks a year per 10,000 people, and differ on the second and fourth components and in how many of their people live in major cities (49%, 1% and 7%).
- **So** the concentration of filing in a minority of advantaged, educated, city areas is the clearest structure in the places lens; the rest is a continuum.

evidence.title: B58: Higher-income areas file more, and individuals there file more for each person who runs a business
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Across postal areas (2023-24), taxable income per individual goes with standard patents per 10,000 people at a rank correlation of 0.384 and with trade marks at 0.453. The share of people with business income goes with filing far less (0.145 and 0.194). Individuals' own applications per 1,000 people with business income rise from a median 3.84 in the most disadvantaged tenth of areas to 11.0 in the most advantaged.

- The second half of the areas agrees: 0.405, 0.518, 0.229 and 0.212.
- Individuals' own filing per person in business barely moves with the share running a business (-0.078; -0.14).
- **So** the advantage gradient is not only that advantaged areas have more business owners.

evidence.text:
Stage 3 tested this with other factors held together.

- **weakened**: With the four components and remoteness held, advantage goes with 1.256 and 1.341 times the standard patent rate per standard deviation, against 1.932 and 2.135 alone (35% and 39% left on a log scale); business density and degrees beyond resources also go with filing, and remoteness stays. section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (2 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Relate taxable income per individual, and the share with business income, to filing rates, in both halves.
2. Divide individuals' own applications by those with business income, and compare by tenth of advantage.

**Which gives observation B58:** Across postal areas (2023-24), taxable income per individual goes with standard patents per 10,000 people at a rank correlation of 0.384 and with trade marks at 0.453. The share of people with business income goes with filing far less (0.145 and 0.194). Individuals' own applications per 1,000 people with business income rise from a median 3.84 in the most disadvantaged tenth of areas to 11.0 in the most advantaged.

evidence.title: B27: Across postal areas the kinds of IP move together, and with education and occupation more than income
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Postal areas that file more standard patents per person also file more provisionals (rank correlation 0.765) and trade marks (0.693). Of the four SEIFA indexes, education and occupation goes with filing most (0.675 with firms with a filing linked per business, 0.455 with standard patents per person); median personal income goes with standard patents at 0.287.

- Areas with more GST-registered businesses per person file more standard patents (0.513; 0.626 in the other half).
- Firms with a filing linked and R&D claimants, per business, are the strongest pair (0.879; 0.894).
- **Claimants with no filing linked are rarer where filing is common:** the share of R&D claimants with no filing linked to their business number falls with designs (-0.253), firms with a filing linked (-0.241) and standard patents (-0.215) per business, and with government suppliers per business (-0.263).
- Rates are shown only where 10 or more applications are expected (U53), so these pairs cover the larger areas (431 areas for standard patents per person in the first half). They compare places, not firms or people.

evidence.title: B30: The advantage gradient is not one firm's; it is at least as strong with each area's largest filer taken out
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Each area's largest filer holds 29.2% of the 24,879 Australian standard patents placed in 2,528 areas. Without it, the rate ratio per standard deviation of advantage is 1.897 (interval 1.74 to 2.067), against 1.717 with it; in the second half, 1.961 against 1.857.

- Single large filers (U52) add noise to areas' counts, not the gradient.
- **Approximate.** A patent joins a filer by its first founding applicant with an ABN, which for a jointly filed patent need not be the party whose postcode places it (about one patent in 20 joined to firms is jointly filed, B26), so "each area's largest filer" is approximate.

evidence.text:
Taking each area's largest filer by the filer's party (the party whose postcode places the patent), the gradient of standard patents with advantage is steeper without it: 1.933 and 2.031 times the rate per standard deviation of IRSAD, against 1.717 and 1.857 with every filer. Stage 2's reading holds with the party-aligned filer.

- 24,879 Australian standard patents placed in 2,528 areas, from 12,793 filers; by the first founding ABN, as B30 took it, the largest filers hold 29.2%.
- Nor do the largest filers account for how far areas differ: the spread beyond chance is larger without them (1.994 and 1.912, against 1.354 and 1.650).

evidence.title: M14: Beyond advantage and remoteness, business density and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
With the four components and remoteness held together, the advantage gradient is still there but weaker: each standard deviation of advantage goes with 1.256 times the standard patent rate, against 1.932 with advantage alone (first half), so 35% to 39% of the raw ratio remains. Two other dimensions go with filing: business density, and degrees and R&D claimants beyond what an area's resources would suggest. Remoteness stays.

- **Trade marks:** 1.830 and 1.362, 51% left (holds, just); 1.988 and 1.386, 48% (weakened). **Designs:** 1.863 and 1.186. **Provisionals:** 1.652 and 1.247. Weakened.
- **Held together, for standard patents:** the second component (older areas, small households, many businesses) 1.446 and 1.219; the third 0.731 and 0.663, so areas with more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources would suggest file more; the fourth 0.702 and 0.666. The same signs for trade marks, designs and provisionals.
- **Remoteness stays:** very remote areas file standard patents at 0.218 and 0.115 of major cities' rate.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Grouping postal areas by their four components gives at most a weak structure: the best grouping, five groups, has a silhouette of 0.269, short of clear segments (0.5 or more). Read as a description, one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas files 3.14 standard patents a year per 10,000 people and holds 13,993 of the 24,879 patents placed (56%); the rest is a continuum.

- Silhouettes for two to eight groups run from 0.232 to 0.269.
- **288 areas** (4,451,909 residents; 95% of their people in major cities; median IRSAD 1,088), high on advantage (1.36) and low on the third component (more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources): 50.13 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
- **713 areas** (11,871,712 residents, the most), above average on advantage (0.78): 0.59 patents and 13.37 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
- **The other three groups** (260, 539 and 725 areas) are below average on advantage and file 0.37 to 0.48 patents and 8.76 to 10.63 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.

- **Components:** the first carries 49.5% of the variation, the first four 82.3% (14.5%, 11.3% and 6.9% for the second to fourth). The first loads on every advantage measure together (IRSAD +0.38, household income +0.36, IEO +0.35, IRSD +0.33, the degree share +0.33): it is the **advantage gradient**. The second rises with median age (+0.52) and businesses per person (+0.46) and falls with household size (-0.47): older areas of small households and many businesses. The third rises with economic resources (IER +0.53) and household size (+0.41) and falls with R&D claimants per 1,000 businesses (-0.46) and the degree share (-0.36): its low end is areas with more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources alone would suggest. evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Fees look a weak lever.** Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after any of nine renewal fee changes (for patents, within about 1.4 points either way), and with trend and season held most filing fee breaks do not behave as prices would. Observations: M28, M34.
- **Among firms, age, form and size go with filing; R&D spend only weakly.** Older R&D claimants and public companies more often have a filing linked, held together; government suppliers that file win about two and a half times the contracts; among large employers the size gap widens within an industry. Spending above the median goes with a standard patent by only 4 to 5 points. Observations: M8, M9, M11, M29.
- **Places: one advantage gradient, and what lies beyond it.** Advantage, income and education are mostly one measure. Beyond it, business density, manufacturing businesses and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing; residents' incomes add nothing detectable; remoteness stays. Observations: M13, M14, M31, M32.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
6,406 area indicators from five sources were set against six filing rates: 24,947 pairs are leads in both halves. Standard patents per person go most with financial and professional businesses per resident, and are lowest where more single mothers receive Parenting Payment; trade marks go most with professional businesses and Year 12 completion.

- Standard patents per person (3,882 leads): financial and insurance businesses with a turnover of $200k to less than $2m per resident (0.595), professional businesses with $2m to less than $5m (0.593); most negative, single mothers receiving Parenting Payment (-0.482) and children whose mothers have low educational attainment (-0.477).

section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (3 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Compare claimants on each of four signals (spend, form, age, place), with nothing held.
2. Fit one model for each outcome (any filing linked; a standard patent) with all four, the state and the postcode's advantage held together.
3. Give each signal's outcome in each half.

**Which gives observation M8:** Among 17,514 active R&D Tax Incentive claimants, claimants 20 years or more on the record are 23.1 points more likely to have a filing linked than those of 3 to 10, with spend, company form, state and postcode advantage held together. Spending above the median and being a public company go with having a standard patent (about 4 to 5 and 8 to 9 points held together), but much less with any filing. A city address goes with filing in one half only.

pool.text:
Across 160 countries of a million people or more (2016 to 2020), residents' patent applications per million people go with business R&D as a share of GDP (rank correlation 0.844), researchers per million (0.837) and GDP per person (0.769). Residents' trade marks go with GDP per person (0.797) and tertiary enrolment (0.804), and much less with R&D: trade marks follow commerce, patents follow research. section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (3 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For each tenth of spend, find the share that has filed a standard patent and the share with no filing linked.
2. Find the share with no filing linked by age, entity group, remoteness and advantage, and who they are together.
3. Check how many of them are linked to IP another way.

**Which gives observation B23:** Among 17,514 active R&D claimants, 9.5% of the lowest-spending tenth have filed a standard patent, rising to 24.1% of the highest-spending tenth. The rank correlation between spend and patent applications is only 0.120. 52% of the lowest spenders and 43.1% of the highest have no IP filing linked to their business number.

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (1 step for this observation, on the places lens)
pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. Australian standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026, placed by the filer's postcode, with the largest filer in each area taken by the filer's party, whether or not it has an ABN.
   - _Why:_ The same party that gives the patent its postcode, as the final review asked.

**Repairs made to the places lens before any observation**

1. Applications are counted at the filer's postcode, not the current holder's.
   - _Why:_ A right sold to a firm elsewhere should stay where it was filed.
2. A rate is shown only where 10 or more applications would be expected at the national rate.
   - _Why:_ A count of 10 has a 95% range of about 5 to 18 by chance alone; below that, an area's rate is mostly noise.
3. Small areas can be pooled into 335 larger ones (SA3s).
   - _Why:_ So that every area's filings count somewhere, even where its own rate is too uncertain to show.
4. Values published for other kinds of area are moved to postal areas by their 2021 residents.
   - _Why:_ A count can be split by where people live; a median or rate is averaged, weighted by the people shared.

pool.title: B47: Changes in the fees to obtain a right seldom moved filing beyond what comparison months show; only one break pointed the way a price would
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
18 changes of 10% or more in the cost of obtaining a right (12 rises, 6 cuts) were set against placebo months: 34 pairs of a change and a filing series. Five moved filing beyond 95% of their placebo months (three rushes and two steps), against about 1.7 of each expected by chance. Only one of the five moved the way a price would: Australians' designs fell after the rise of July 1988. The clearest breaks came with new Acts, the Trade Marks Act 1995 and the Designs Act 2003.

- **How a price would push:** filing brought forward before a rise and lower after it; before a cut, filing would wait, and rise after it.
- **The Trade Marks Act 1995** (January 1996): filing by Australians and overseas applicants fell before the rise (2.778% of placebo months as large), which is the Act's pause (B37), not a price.
- **Overseas applicants' standard patents** were filed early before the 15.31% cut of January 1998 (2.778%), the opposite of what a price would do.
- **The Designs Act 2003** (June 2004, a design's filing fee up 122.2%): overseas applicants' designs stepped up (none of 72 placebo months as large), against a price; that is the Act (B37).

events.answer:
Yes—**more advantaged postal areas tend to file more standard patents per person**. The association remains when other area characteristics are held together, but it becomes substantially weaker: that is Stage 3’s **M14 (observational)** finding.[1]

### How strong is the pattern?
**B29 (Stage 2, observational)** found that each standard deviation higher on the area advantage score went with **1.717 times** as many standard patents per person in one half of the areas, and **1.857** in the other half.[2] A standard deviation is a way of measuring a step up the advantage scale relative to how widely areas differ.

The pattern is not a steady climb: standard patent filing runs from **0.33 to 0.75 a year per 10,000 people across deciles 1 to 8**, then **1.51 to 1.62 in deciles 9 and 10**—so much of the difference sits at the most advantaged end.[3]

### What did the further checks find?
- **The link weakens, but remains.** M14 held together advantage, age and business density, degrees beyond resources, rent and remoteness. The advantage ratios were then **1.256 and 1.341**, compared with **1.932 and 2.135** when advantage was considered alone in that analysis; the atlas labels the result **weakened**.[4]
- **It is not just a few dominant filers.** **M15 (Stage 3, observational)** found that removing each area’s largest filer made the advantage gradient steeper, confirming the earlier B30 finding with a more accurately aligned filer measure.[5]
- **Advantage overlaps with other characteristics.** **M13 (Stage 3, descriptive)** found that income, education and other advantage measures largely describe the same broad gradient; none should be read as the single factor that matters.[6]

**The takeaway:** patent filing and area advantage go together, but this is an observational comparison between places—not evidence that making a place more advantaged would itself produce more patents.[7] Holding measured factors together helps separate overlapping patterns; it does not rule out explanations involving factors the analysis has not held together.

pool.text:
Of the 23,971 firms that filed standard patents, the top 1% filed 55.3% of them, while the typical (median) firm filed just one. Trade marks are less concentrated: the top 1% of filing firms filed 25.7%.

- **Standard patents.** 23,971 firms filed 183,989; the median firm filed 1 and the 90th percentile firm 7.
- **Trade marks.** 301,249 firms filed 1,018,160; median 1, 90th percentile 6; the top 1% filed 25.7%.
- **Designs.** 14,113 firms filed 77,794, and the top 1% filed 35.6%. Provisional applications: the top 1% of 24,905 firms filed 32.0%. Second-tier patents: the top 1% of 6,077 firms filed 12.2%.
- **What firms hold now.** 260,292 firms hold 1,262,125 rights; 116,240 hold 430,305 rights still in force, and the top 1% of those hold 28.7%.

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the research institutions lens)
pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. Each university's standard patents over a period as a negative binomial model with its works as the exposure (so the result is patents per work).
   - _Why:_ Compares rates without dividing every measure by the same number.
2. Citations per work and the share of works cited by patents are each compared with works of the same publication year (fixed age).
   - _Why:_ A 2012 work has had longer to be cited than a 2021 one; the final review asked for fixed-age windows.

**Repairs made to the research institutions lens before any observation**

1. Institutions are linked to rights, grants and contracts through a reviewed list of 116 extra names and 146 ABNs.
   - _Why:_ Universities file under former names, predecessors' names and their commercialisation companies' names.
2. An institution's works and citations are its own, never added across institutions or from a child to its parent.
   - _Why:_ A paper with authors at two institutions counts for both.

pool.title: B23: More R&D spend goes with patenting, but only weakly; about half of R&D claimants have no IP filing linked to their business number, at any level of spend
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Among 17,514 active R&D claimants, 9.5% of the lowest-spending tenth have filed a standard patent, rising to 24.1% of the highest-spending tenth. The rank correlation between spend and patent applications is only 0.120. 52% of the lowest spenders and 43.1% of the highest have no IP filing linked to their business number.

- The lowest tenth spends a median $44,790 a year; the highest $3.79m.
- **No filing linked** is most common among claimants under 3 years old on the record (72.9%) and least among those 20 years or more (32.6%); more common in private companies (49.2%) than public ones (36.2%), and in outer regional areas (60.3%) than major cities (48%). It does not rise or fall in step with the postcode's advantage.
- **Who they are, together:** 55.3% of the 8,444 are private companies 3 to 10 years old on the record; only 2.4% are under 3.
- **Another link to IP explains little of it:** of the claimants with no filing linked, 10.9% of those 20 years or more, and 4.1% of those under 3, are linked to IP another way (holding a right, another IP record, or an older IP Australia dataset).

evidence.title: M40: Asking for examination before being directed goes with patents more likely to end, not less, against IP Australia's commissioned study
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
IP Australia's commissioned study counts a request for examination made before the Commissioner directs one as a way of speeding examination up, and reports that applicants who speed up are more likely to renew their patents. Built from the open data, the same measure covers 41.39% of granted patents (the study: 41.9%). But with the filer, field, route, cohort and expedited examination held together, those patents are more likely to end in a given year after grant, in both periods (hazard ratios 1.276 and 1.383).

- **The measure reproduces the study's share:** 303,486 standard patents with a date of patent in 2004 to 2016, divisionals left out, of which 191,477 granted; 41.28% were never directed. The share rose between the periods: overseas organisations 0.273 to 0.5148, Australian organisations 0.2357 to 0.4602.
- **By filer, held together:** overseas organisations 1.282, then 1.388; overseas individuals 1.298, then 1.340; Australian organisations 1.005 (not detected either way), then 1.587; Australian individuals 1.169 (not detected once held), then 1.486.

- **One reading, to test:** applicants who wait use the years to drop weak applications before grant, the study's own point about delay as an option, so the granted patents of those who were directed are already filtered.

evidence.text: - **M40: Disputed in part.** Evidence: Added with A36 (section 11.8). The commissioned study (ipr-2025 p9, p10, p13): applicants who speed up examination, including by asking for it early and unprompted (41.9% of granted patents), are more likely to renew, commercialise and build on their patents. The lens reproduces the measure (41.39%, section 11.2), but with the filer, field, route, cohort, co-filers, classes and expedited examination held, those patents are more likely to end in a given year after grant (hazard ratios 1.276 and 1.383) What follows: The study's outcome and model are not in IP Australia's report, so this disputes its direction on its own measure, not its model; a question proposed for IP Australia (OQ28) Note: Disputed in part. IP Australia's commissioned study's measure is reproduced (41.39% of granted patents asked for examination before any direction, against its 41.9%), but those patents are more likely to end, not less, with who filed, the field and the route held (1.276 and 1.383). The study's own model is not published, so it is its direction on its measure that is disputed.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Asking for examination sooner is not a sign of a longer life.** Expedited examination's link with staying in force does not survive the filer, field and route held together, and Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year. On the wider measure IP Australia's commissioned study uses, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383), against the study's finding. Observations: M5, M40.
- **Some Australian invention ends up owned overseas, by two routes.** Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type, and so are patents filed before the firm's first registration. Inventions made here and filed from overseas come in about equal numbers from international teams and from all-Australian ones. Observations: M6, M27, M30.
- **The same organisations file more divisionals.** Divisionals doubled within the same filers (+19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones), not through a change in fields or filers. Observations: M26.

**M40 found that patents whose applicants requested examination before being directed to do so were more likely to end after grant—not less likely.** This Stage 3 finding is observational: the association remained when the filer, technology field, filing route, cohort and expedited examination were held together. [1]

### What the analysis showed
The early, unprompted request measure covered **41.39%** of granted standard patents from **2004 to 2016**, close to the commissioned study’s **41.9%**. [2] M40 then compared patents from grant onwards, so the comparison was between patents still alive at the same age. [3]

The adjusted hazard ratios—the relative likelihood of a patent ending in a given year while still in force—were:
- **1.276** for **FY2010 to FY2016**. [4]
- **1.383** for **FY2003 to FY2009**. [5]

A hazard ratio above one means a higher likelihood of ending, rather than a longer life. M40 refined the earlier observational signal in B13: on this wider measure of speeding up examination, the link with longer patent life was not found. [6]

### Why the result matters—and its limits
The result points in the opposite direction to the commissioned study’s reported association between speeding up examination and renewing patents. However, the atlas labels this **“disputed in part”**: the study’s outcome definition and model are not published in IP Australia’s report, so M40 disputes the direction on the same measure, rather than reproducing and rejecting the study’s exact model. [7]

One possible explanation, explicitly put forward for testing, is that applicants who wait drop weaker applications before grant, leaving a more selected group of granted patents among those who were directed to request examination. That is a possible reading, not an established finding. [8] Holding measured factors together does not make this an experiment: the result does **not** show that requesting examination early causes a patent to end sooner.

The proposed next step is to ask IP Australia how the commissioned study measured renewal lifetime and which factors it held together, and to read M40 alongside M5. [9]
