evidence.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Of the standard patents Australian individuals filed alone in FY2010 to FY2019, 4.8% were granted, against 40.6% of those filed with an attorney: a gap of 35.8 points (interval 33.9 to 37.5). In FY2000 to FY2009 the gap was 36.8 points. It stays among applications whose examination was requested (34.4 points).

- **Filing alone goes with not asking for examination:** 25.2% of individuals' lone applications were examined, against 75.9% with an attorney.
- **Australian organisations do not show it in both decades:** a gap of 40.0 points in FY2010 to FY2019 but -6.0 in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,149 applications organisations filed alone were granted 62.1% of the time. Those earlier lone filers may have been firms with their own patent staff; the data do not say.
- **Trade marks show it in both decades, for both:** with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more often, organisations' 23.6 points.

evidence.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Designs cannot be read here:** the comparison keeps only designs with a known filer, and IP RAPID gives no origin for nearly every design that lapsed or was withdrawn (B3), so its 99.4% to 100% registered reflects that selection, not designs' registration rate.
- **Not a cause.** Representation counts an agent recorded at any time, so an application dropped early may never appoint one (the arrow can run backwards); and those who file alone differ in resources and experience.

evidence.title: M1: Patents filed without an attorney are still granted far less often once the factors settled at filing are held together
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often than those filed with an attorney once the route, filing year, state and co-filers are held together (FY2010 to FY2019), against 35.8 points with nothing held: 87.2% of Stage 2's gap remains, and 86.2% in the earlier decade. Trade marks filed alone show the same gap for individuals and organisations alike, almost untouched by what is held.

- **Australian organisations' patents** hold in FY2010 to FY2019 (-40.0 raw, -35.3 held together) but not in FY2000 to FY2009, where neither the raw nor the held figure is detected (+6.0, interval -18.5 to 30.6). That decade's 1,149 lone applications came from 392 filers, the ten largest filing 59.8% of them: a few heavy filers, perhaps with their own patent staff, though the data do not say who they were.
- **A second reading** among applications that have a technology field, holding the field and number of classes too: -27.2 and -27.8 points. Among examined applications: -30.5 and -29.1.

evidence.title: M1: Patents filed without an attorney are still granted far less often once the factors settled at filing are held together
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Not a few filers' doing.** The ten heaviest lone filers hold 0.8% to 10.1% of the lone filings in every group but the older organisations'; Australian individuals' 1,642 lone patent applications came from 1,370 filers.
- **Not a cause.** Only what is known at filing is held. The filer's resources, experience and the merit of the invention are not in the data, and an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney, so the arrow can run backwards.

section: Early signals that warrant further investigation
evidence.text:
Stage 3's first table, for the research owner's review (section 8 of the Stage 3 notebook). Each signal is an association that survived its third factors held together, in both samples unless marked; none is a cause, and adopting any as a conclusion is the owner's decision.

- **Filing alone goes with far fewer grants (Australian individuals' standard patents, about 31 points), and no agent before the first renewal with fewer trade marks and designs in force after it, with the factors settled at filing held.** Observations: B5, B6, B10, M1, M2. Strength: Observational, holds in both decades. Questions: Q2, Q4. Next: A design that separates the choice of an attorney from the outcome: the same filers' applications with and without one, or a change in what representation costs.
- **Within the same reach, Australian organisations' patents are less likely to end, yet reach fewer offices and are cited less at the same field, route and year.** Observations: B8, B11, B12, B55, M3, M4. Strength: Observational (three readings that disagree) Questions: Q1. Next: Validate each as a sign of value against licensing, litigation or sale; read the three together, never one alone.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Every Stage 3 page follows the same five steps, and shows the first three at its top as a chain: what Stage 2 found, what was held together, and what is left.

- **Start from a Stage 2 signal.** Signal. Sub-questions: A pair that held in two samples. A pair of measures that went together in Stage 2, in a first sample and again in a second: for example, filing without an attorney and fewer grants (B6).
- **Name its third factors.** Third factors. Sub-questions: What else could explain it. Stage 2 named, for each signal, the other factors that could make the two measures go together: the route of filing, the year, the field, the filer's type, a place's advantage.
- **Hold them together.** Held. Sub-questions: One model, every factor at once. One model holds every named factor fixed at once, so the signal is read among rights, firms or places alike in all of them. Intervals allow a filer's many rights to be alike, or resample neighbouring quarters in blocks.
- **Compare raw and held.** Compare. Sub-questions: How much of the signal is left. The raw figure (Stage 2's comparison, with nothing held) is set beside the held one. The charts show both: grey for raw, blue for held, each with its 95% interval.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
What Stage 3 found

Stage 3 took each signal Stage 2 carried forward and held its named third factors together in one model, to see how much of it is left. The bar counts every check by its outcome; the list gives the findings most worth knowing. All are associations or descriptions, not causes.

Stage 2 found pairs of measures that move together and named, for each, the other factors that might explain it. Stage 3 holds those factors together, signal by signal, and says how much of each is left. It also asks what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. This page sets out how the test works, what its outcomes mean, and every check it made, each linked to its page.

**Held is not controlled.** Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive, and none answers a research question yet. Its two tables, early signals and data gaps, await the research owner's review.

Yes—**B6’s main finding survived Stage 3**, with the outcome **“holds”** in M1 (observational): Australian individuals’ standard patents filed without an attorney were still granted substantially less often once filing route, year, state and co-filers were held together. [1]

- **FY2010 to FY2019:** the gap was 31.2 points after those factors were held together, compared with 35.8 points before; 87.2% of the original gap remained. [2]
- **FY2000 to FY2009:** the gap also held, at 31.7 points after holding those factors together, compared with 36.8 points before. [3]

For B6’s related comparisons, M1 found that the trade mark gap held for both individuals and organisations, while Australian organisations’ patent gap held in FY2010 to FY2019 only—not in FY2000 to FY2009. [4]

**That strengthens the association, not a causal claim.** M1 could not account for filers’ resources, experience or the merit of their inventions. Also, applications dropped early may never appoint an attorney, so the direction of the link can run backwards. [5] Stage 3’s findings still await the research owner’s review. [6]

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
FY2026 had 10,069 provisional applications, against 4,143 to 5,047 a year in FY2022 to FY2025. In 5,510 the first applicant named at filing was an individual, against 1,413 to 1,986 a year before; in 4,558 it was an organisation, against 2,751 (FY2024) and 3,060 (FY2025). The rise began in early 2025, peaked in March and April 2026, and had eased by September 2026.

- **When.** 345 in March 2024, 481 in March 2025, 1,274 in March 2026 and 1,231 in April 2026, then 750 by September 2026, still about twice March 2024's level.
- **Broad.** Individuals who filed a single provisional rose from 1,538 (FY2025) to 2,507 (FY2026).
- **And concentrated.** 54 individuals filed 10 or more each (1,528 between them), against 9 who filed 183 in FY2025; one filed 375. 45 organisations filed 10 or more (1,258), against 24 (566).

**Repairs made to the IP rights lens before any observation**

**Held together (raw and adjusted).** A comparison made inside one model with several third factors at once, so that each is held fixed while the others are too. pool.text:
What Stage 3 found

Stage 3 took each signal Stage 2 carried forward and held its named third factors together in one model, to see how much of it is left. The bar counts every check by its outcome; the list gives the findings most worth knowing. All are associations or descriptions, not causes.

Stage 2 found pairs of measures that move together and named, for each, the other factors that might explain it. Stage 3 holds those factors together, signal by signal, and says how much of each is left. It also asks what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. This page sets out how the test works, what its outcomes mean, and every check it made, each linked to its page.

**Held is not controlled.** Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive, and none answers a research question yet. Its two tables, early signals and data gaps, await the research owner's review.

events.answer:
**U8’s simple message is that provisional applications surged in FY2026, mostly from individuals—but organisations filed more too.** This is a **Stage 1 descriptive finding**: it shows what changed, not why. [1]

A provisional is a low-cost placeholder, not a granted patent. So more provisionals should not be read as more granted patents. [2]

### What changed?
- **The total roughly doubled:** there were 10,069 provisional applications in FY2026, compared with 4,143 to 5,047 a year in FY2022 to FY2025. [3]
- **Individuals accounted for most of the rise:** 5,510 applications named an individual as the first applicant, compared with 1,413 to 1,986 a year before. [4]
- **Organisations also contributed:** their count reached 4,558, up from 3,060 in FY2025. [4]

U8 shows that the rise was both **broad and concentrated**. Individuals filing just one provisional became more numerous: 2,507 in FY2026, compared with 1,538 in FY2025. But there was also a group filing many applications: 54 individuals filed 10 or more each, accounting for 1,528 applications between them; one individual filed 375. [5]

The rise began in early 2025, peaked in March and April 2026, and had eased by September 2026. [6]

### Were those applications followed through?
**Stage 3’s M35, an observational finding, adds a caution—but its follow-up results concern FY2025, not the full FY2026 surge.** Australian individuals’ provisionals were followed by a complete application within 12 months 6.66% of the time in FY2025, against 12.91% in FY2022 to FY2024. [7]

M35 found that the fall remained when the filer’s state, filing volume, filing history and filing month were held together. Among individuals who also filed in the earlier years, however, a fall was not detected: the decline was concentrated in new and heavy filers. This is an observational result, not proof of a cause. [8]

### What remains unclear?
U8 does **not explain why filing surged**: possible explanations such as new filing channels, costs or drafting tools are not tested in these data. [9] Nor is lower recorded follow-up necessarily abandonment: late recording and international follow-up routes remain unresolved limitations in M35. [10]

**The takeaway:** U8 records a sharp change in filing activity, not evidence by itself of more granted patents or greater value from the system. Its follow-up evidence is a reason to investigate what happened, rather than settle the explanation. [11]

evidence.title: Glossary: Held together (raw and adjusted)
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
**Held together (raw and adjusted).** A comparison made inside one model with several third factors at once, so that each is held fixed while the others are too. The raw figure is the plain comparison Stage 2 made, with nothing held; the difference between the two is how much of the raw figure those factors account for.

Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
What Stage 3 found

Stage 3 took each signal Stage 2 carried forward and held its named third factors together in one model, to see how much of it is left. The bar counts every check by its outcome; the list gives the findings most worth knowing. All are associations or descriptions, not causes.

Stage 2 found pairs of measures that move together and named, for each, the other factors that might explain it. Stage 3 holds those factors together, signal by signal, and says how much of each is left. It also asks what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. This page sets out how the test works, what its outcomes mean, and every check it made, each linked to its page.

**Held is not controlled.** Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive, and none answers a research question yet. Its two tables, early signals and data gaps, await the research owner's review.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Every Stage 3 page follows the same five steps, and shows the first three at its top as a chain: what Stage 2 found, what was held together, and what is left.

- **Start from a Stage 2 signal.** Signal. Sub-questions: A pair that held in two samples. A pair of measures that went together in Stage 2, in a first sample and again in a second: for example, filing without an attorney and fewer grants (B6).
- **Name its third factors.** Third factors. Sub-questions: What else could explain it. Stage 2 named, for each signal, the other factors that could make the two measures go together: the route of filing, the year, the field, the filer's type, a place's advantage.
- **Hold them together.** Held. Sub-questions: One model, every factor at once. One model holds every named factor fixed at once, so the signal is read among rights, firms or places alike in all of them. Intervals allow a filer's many rights to be alike, or resample neighbouring quarters in blocks.
- **Compare raw and held.** Compare. Sub-questions: How much of the signal is left. The raw figure (Stage 2's comparison, with nothing held) is set beside the held one. The charts show both: grey for raw, blue for held, each with its 95% interval.

evidence.title: Limits and assumptions
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: What the three stages cannot tell you
evidence.text:
- **Why.** Stage 1's observations are descriptive and Stage 2's are associations. Stage 3 holds the measured third factors together, which is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain a link, and some links may run backwards (an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney, B6, M1). Causal claims need designs, such as natural experiments, that come after the exploration.
- **What "not detected" means.** When Stage 3 says a link is not detected once held, its interval includes no difference. That is not evidence of no link: with 19 industries, about 40 universities or 36 countries, a moderate link can go undetected. Only for patents' renewal at each anniversary is the null precise (within about 1.4 points, M28).
- **Value.** Counts of rights, lifetimes, reach and citations are measures of activity and private value, not of public value. The research goal treats them as indicators, never as success.
- **People from places.** Stage 2's pairs across postal areas and countries describe the areas and countries, not the people or firms in them. Areas with more graduates file more; that does not show the graduates are the filers.

evidence.title: Glossary: Holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed
evidence.text:
**Holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed.** Stage 3's words for what is left of a signal once its third factors are held together. Holds: the same direction, its 95% interval clear of no difference, and at least half of the raw size left. Weakened: the same direction and clear, but less than half left. Not detected once held: the interval includes no difference. Reversed: the other direction, and clear.

Where the raw figure was not itself detected: appears once held (the held one is clear) or not detected either way. "Does not replicate" marks a result seen in one sample but not the second; "mixed", a page whose parts differ; and "refined", a description that sharpens an earlier one. Ratios are compared on a log scale (ADR 0046). Not detected is not the same as no association: a moderate one may be missed.

evidence.title: Limits and assumptions
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- Stage 2 measures every pair on one scale from 0 to 1 and calls a pair a lead only if it reaches 0.1, survives the correction for the number of pairs, holds in a second period or sample, and is not two versions of one measure (ADR 0030).
- Stage 3 calls a signal held if, with its third factors held together, it keeps its direction, its 95% interval is clear of no difference and at least half of its raw size is left (ADR 0046). A filer's rights are one source of evidence (clustered by the filer's party), and quarterly changes are resampled in blocks.

evidence.title: What comes next
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: - **Stage 3, many variables together.** When: First pass done (3 November 2026); tables await the owner's review. Asks: Do the signals survive once other factors are held together? What structure and groups exist? How: Each signal Stage 2 carried was modelled with its named third factors held together, and its raw and held figures compared (holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed). The methods the final review asked for were used throughout: intervals that allow a filer's rights to be alike, block resampling of quarterly changes, citations counted at a fixed age, industry comparisons through the crosswalk with services, and research spend as a base. Places' and countries' characteristics were reduced to a few components, and places grouped to see whether they form kinds. Example: Is an area's patent rate still linked to advantage once its business mix and education are allowed for? Yes, but weaker: 35% to 39% of the ratio is left, and business density and degrees beyond resources matter too (M14). Adds: Separates signals that hold from ones explained by something else, and produces two tables: fifteen early signals, with their evidence and strength, and thirteen data gaps, with possible sources and costs. Done when: When the owner has reviewed the two tables and decided on the name match (OQ26).

evidence.text:
- **Descriptive.** Stages: 1; 2; 3. What the data show. How much, how often, for whom. No claim about why.
- **Observational.** Stages: 2; 3. Things go together, even with other factors held. There may be other explanations. Stages 2 and 3 produce these.
- **Causal.** One thing causes another. Needs a design, such as a natural experiment, that this exploration does not have.
- **Projected.** An estimate of the future, with its assumptions stated. Belongs to Question 5.

**3. What is left**

events.answer:
**Holding factors together means comparing like with like on several measured characteristics at once.** The atlas puts those factors into one model, so a comparison is made among rights, firms or places that are alike on all the named factors—not just one at a time. [1]

### What the comparison tells us
Two measures can go together because of something else—a **third factor**. For example, firm size could help explain why firms with intellectual property (IP) also win larger contracts, without IP itself causing the difference. [2]

Stage 2 identifies pairs of measures that go together and names possible third factors; Stage 3 then holds those factors together and checks how much of the original association remains. [3] The atlas calls the original comparison **raw** and the comparison with factors held together **adjusted**; the difference shows how much of the raw association those measured factors account for. [4]

### Why it is not an experiment
**Making the groups more comparable does not establish what caused the difference.** Unmeasured factors can still explain the association, and the link may run in the opposite direction from what we first imagine. [5]

B6 and its Stage 3 follow-up, M1, illustrate this limit: M1 found that the observational link between filing without an attorney and fewer grants **holds** after the named factors are held together. [6] But an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney—so the lack of an attorney could partly reflect early abandonment, rather than explain it. [7] The finding therefore does not establish that help with filing would raise grant rates; that claim needs a further research design. [8]

A causal test needs a design that can distinguish what a change itself did from other explanations; the atlas says this exploration does not have such a design. [9] Its glossary gives a natural experiment as one possibility: a real event, such as a policy change, affects some people but not others, allowing a comparison of what the change itself did. [10]

In short: **holding factors together tests whether an association survives some alternative explanations; it does not rule out every alternative explanation.** All Stage 3 findings remain observational or descriptive, not causal. [11]

pool.title: B34: Across OECD members patenting rises with business R&D almost one for one, but changes in R&D barely go with changes in patenting
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Across 36 members, residents' patents per person rise with business R&D (rank correlation 0.853; a slope of 1.151 on log scales). Australia filed 103.3 applications per million people in 2016 to 2020, about what its R&D predicts (98.46). But across members the change in patenting over the decade goes with the change in business R&D at only 0.165.

- In 2006 to 2010 Australia filed 125 against 226.3 predicted (55.22%). The prediction intervals are wide (17 to 580), so Australia is within the members' range in both periods: its change in position came from falling R&D, not rising patenting.
- 23 members' residents filed less over the decade. Australia's patenting fell from 125 to 103.3 per million (about 17%) as its business R&D fell by 0.34 points of GDP.
- **So** the strong link is between countries' levels, which share a long history; within a decade the changes were not seen to move together (0.165 over 34 members).

evidence.text:
- **Fees look a weak lever.** Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after any of nine renewal fee changes (for patents, within about 1.4 points either way), and with trend and season held most filing fee breaks do not behave as prices would. Observations: M28, M34.
- **Among firms, age, form and size go with filing; R&D spend only weakly.** Older R&D claimants and public companies more often have a filing linked, held together; government suppliers that file win about two and a half times the contracts; among large employers the size gap widens within an industry. Spending above the median goes with a standard patent by only 4 to 5 points. Observations: M8, M9, M11, M29.
- **Places: one advantage gradient, and what lies beyond it.** Advantage, income and education are mostly one measure. Beyond it, business density, manufacturing businesses and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing; residents' incomes add nothing detectable; remoteness stays. Observations: M13, M14, M31, M32.

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Policy changes broke series as the law required; few breaks show behaviour, and fee changes rarely moved filing.** Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month, but most of those breaks were certain by law. The rush before Raising the Bar is the clearest sign of applicants' behaviour. Of the changes in fees to obtain a right, only one break went the way a price would; of the changes in renewal fees, only one (trade marks, July 1993) survives every check. Observations: B37, B47, B49.
- **Women's share among inventors varies by field more than by filer.** From 4.2% in civil engineering to 26.9% in biotechnology, an order that holds across decades. On provisional applications, Australian organisations' inventors include more women than Australian individuals'. Observations: B17, B18.
- **Across industries, the patents allocated by technology follow R&D once services are counted.** Industry counts are applications allocated by what they protect, not what each industry's businesses file. Through the crosswalk with services, patents allocated per business follow business R&D per business. A division's share of innovating businesses showed no clear pattern with patenting in three surveys. Observations: B53, B54, B42, B60.

section: How this moves the research forward
evidence.text:
Stage 2 answers none of the five questions either: it finds which measures go together. This is how the association prepares the ground for them.

- **Q4. Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?** Official fees are IP Australia's most direct lever. Past changes in the fees to obtain a right seldom moved national filing beyond the ordinary, but the changes are few and several coincide with new Acts, so this cannot show how much fees matter.
- **Q5. What outcomes could interventions produce?** Fee changes are candidate natural experiments, but most are small and some are confounded with Acts.

_Linking an observation to a question is the analyst's guide to where it may help. It is not a finding._

pool.text:
Stage 1 answers none of the five questions. This is how the observation prepares the ground for them.

- **Q1. What public value does the IP system create?** How often applications succeed is part of what the system costs applicants and what it delivers.
- **Q4. Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?** Changes in grant rates may follow changes in law or practice, which IP Australia controls.

_Linking an observation to a question is the analyst's guide to where it may help. It is not a finding._

pool.title: M6: Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Of standard patents first filed by an Australian applicant, the granted are more often now held only overseas than those never granted, with reach, the filer's type, field, route, year and co-filers held together: +5.6 points (FY2003 to FY2011) and +2.8 (FY2012 to FY2021). The wide patents' higher rate is more than halved once grant and type are held, and organisations' gap goes in the later period.

- **Granted against never granted:** +8.8 raw and +5.6 held together; +3.9 and +2.8. Holds in both, 63.9% and 70.4% left.
- **Five or more offices against Australia only:** +10.8 and +4.3; +5.1 and +2.2. Weakened: much of the wide patents' higher rate goes with their being granted and organisations'.
- **Organisations against individuals:** +5.3 and +2.6, weakened; +1.0 and +0.05, not detected once held in the later period.
- **Two endpoints, not transfers:** grant and reach are seen today, not necessarily before the holder changed, and nothing here says where value goes. The later period has had less time for holders to change.

pool.title: U27: Patent grants peaked in 2016; trade mark cessations reached their highest in 2025
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Patent grants peaked at 25,687 in 2016, three years after the rush to file before Raising the Bar, and were 19,612 in 2025. Trade mark registrations reached 70,634 in 2021. Trade mark cessations (registered marks let go) rose from 7,240 in 1996 to 35,484 in 2025, the peak, though not steadily: 29,802 in 2019 and 28,319 in 2023.

- Patent expiries rose from 30 (1996) to 4,019 (2025), as patents filed under the 20-year term reach it.
- Ownership transfers: trade mark assignments peaked at 18,370 (2019), patent assignments at 6,015 (2015).
- Trade mark oppositions rose from 824 (1996) to 2,309 (2025, the peak).
- Trade mark cessations fell to 3,773 in 2002 while lapses rose: accounted for by the gap between two Acts' first terms and the large filing year of 2000 (U38).

events.answer:
The atlas does not establish that IP Australia should cut patent fees for small businesses. That is a policy recommendation, which is outside its scope. Its evidence suggests that past official fee changes have generally been a weak lever—but the passages do not test a fee cut targeted at small businesses.[1]

### What the evidence says

- **Renewal fees:** Stage 3’s **M28 (observational)** found no detected change in owners letting patents, trade marks or designs lapse after any of nine renewal fee changes from 2000, once trends and other named factors were held together. For patents, the uncertainty intervals rule out changes larger than about 1.4 points either way.[2] That is fairly precise evidence of little response in the patent renewals tested—not proof that every possible fee cut would have no effect.
- **Fees to obtain a right:** Stage 3’s **M34 (observational)** found that, after accounting for trend and season, most filing-fee breaks did not behave as a straightforward price response would suggest.[3] For the January 1998 patent fee cut, overseas applicants brought filing forward before the cut and filed more afterwards; no response was detected for Australian applicants. The earlier filing runs against a simple price explanation, while the rise afterwards points in its favour.[4]
- **Why the later tests matter:** Stage 2’s **B49 (observational)** had identified rises in cessations around some renewal fee changes. The Stage 3 follow-up found that the national-series rise for patents did not mean owners were more likely to abandon a patent at its renewal anniversary: more patents reached those anniversaries, rather than more being let go.[5]

### What that means for this decision

My reading of the exploratory evidence is that **a broad expectation of substantially more filing or retention from lower fees is not well supported by these historical tests**.[6] But the atlas itself cautions that the filing-fee changes are few and several coincide with new Acts, limiting what they reveal about how much fees matter.[7]

There is also a cost boundary: *official fees* are what IP Australia charges to file, examine, register and renew rights; they exclude attorneys’ fees, which are often larger.[8] These passages therefore do not establish whether official fees are the important barrier for small businesses.

This remains exploratory evidence, not a settled answer about where to intervene. Answering the atlas’s intervention questions awaits the research owner’s review of Stage 3.

evidence.title: Checked against IP Australia
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: - **U45: Consistent; the lead's reading supported.** Evidence: IP Australia: resident trade marks reached a record 55,913 in 2025, +15.1% (ipr-2026 p39; lens 55,759). Counted by applicant, which needs no ABN, first-time resident trade mark filers rose from 22,838 (2024) to 28,626 (2025) in the lens (context.csv), while those linked to an ABN fell (U45: 11,318 in FY2024 to 7,384 in FY2026) What follows: The fall is in ABN linking, not in filing; firm filing by year still stops at FY2024 until IP Australia says why (OQ7) Note: IP Australia reports record trade mark filings by Australians in 2025 (55,913). Counted by applicant rather than by ABN, first-time Australian trade mark filers rose from 22,838 in 2024 to 28,626 in 2025. So most of the fall this observation found is in linking filers to their ABNs, not in filing; IP Australia's own register restores most of the link (U100), and first observed filers are now counted with it (U101).

evidence.title: M39: Trade marks and real GDP share a long-run path and trade marks run a quarter ahead, but the lead is small and not detected since 2008
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
IP Australia's analytical note finds trade mark filings sharing a long-run path with real GDP and leading it. From 1983 to 2023 the two are cointegrated here too (p 0.018), and in levels more trade marks go with more GDP a quarter or two later. But in changes, with GDP's own growth held, 10% faster growth in trade marks goes with only about 0.38 points faster GDP growth the next quarter (0.038, interval 0.014 to 0.063), and the lead is not detected after 2008.

- **By period:** before 2008, 0.019 (0.005 to 0.033), p 0.017; after, 0.048 (-0.016 to 0.113), p 0.316, not detected. The shared path is clear after 2008 (p 0.005) but not before (0.181).
- **By origin:** the two lags are clear for overseas applicants' trade marks over the whole span (p 0.003) and for Australians' before 2008 (p 0.003).
- **The other way round:** GDP's growth does not lead trade marks over 1983 to 2023 (p 0.718); after 2008 it goes against them (-1.402), the pandemic's boom in trade marks while GDP fell, which the note calls countercyclical.

evidence.title: U70: The United States files about four in ten patent applications at IP Australia; China now files as many as Australians
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Of patent applications at IP Australia, the United States filed 41.2% in 1995, 45.6% in 2004 and 41.9% in 2024. Australians filed 12.7%, 11.2% and 8.3%; China 0.0%, 0.3% and 8.3%. Three-quarters of Australians' own applications (76.1% in 2024) are made abroad.

- IP Australia beside other OECD offices (2024): 405 patent examiners (median office 83.5); 347 days from an examination request to the first action (median 210); trade marks 37 days to the first action (median 30).
- WIPO gives IP Australia's average time to register a trade mark as 222 days (2016), the peak found in IP RAPID (U11). So the peak is consistent with the office's usual path to registration; WIPO's figure is an average, and IP RAPID's mean for FY2010 to FY2019 is 286.5 days.
- Australian residents' applications at every office were 4,389 (1995), 10,631 (2005) and 10,633 (2024), against 1,784, 2,555 and 2,542 at IP Australia.

evidence.text:
- What evidence supports IP Australia's reading that digital tools, including AI, drove the rise in provisional applications, and are the few very heavy filers part of it? (OQ5, U8, M35)
- IP Australia's register records "Examination expedited" for nearly every trade mark claiming an overseas filing date, and for a growing share of other marks where no one asked; IP RAPID stopped publishing the event in November 2018. What does it mean where no one asked, and could IP RAPID publish it? (OQ6, U34)
- IP Australia's register holds a business number for most of the recent applications that have none in IP RAPID. Why does IP RAPID leave them out, and could it publish them? (OQ7, U45, M12)
- What does IP Australia's figure of 55.6% of resident applications filed by individuals in 2022 count? (OQ12, U13, U48)
- IP Australia's own register, IP RAPID and WIPO agree on 2018's trade marks, about 2,000 fewer than IP Australia's report: what did the report's 2018 count include? (OQ13, U5)

evidence.text:
- But the share of Australian organisations' trade marks with a filer's ABN fell from 84.1% (FY2024) to 71.4% (FY2025) and 59.9% (FY2026); for designs from 88.4% to 76.3%, for standard patents from 88.7% to 83.9%. So at least part of the fall was in linking, not filing.

evidence.title: U100: With the register's business numbers, the share of filings linked to an ABN falls only slightly after July 2024
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
In IP RAPID, Australian organisations' trade marks with the filer's ABN fell from 84.1% in FY2024 to 59.9% in FY2026. Filled from IP Australia's register, the share is 92.3% in FY2024, 91.4% in FY2025 and 90.9% in FY2026. So most of the fall is in what IP RAPID publishes, not in the firms filing. Shares are of applications, not of distinct firms.

- Designs: 88.4% against 92.3% filled (FY2024), 76.3% against 89.3% (FY2026).
- The register itself records more business numbers in recent years: of the trade marks IP RAPID leaves without one, it fills 23% to 29.2% of those filed to FY2019, 44.5% to 51.9% in FY2022 to FY2024, and 69.9% and 77.4% in FY2025 and FY2026. So the filled share is comparable from FY2024 on, and a lower bound earlier.
- Why IP RAPID lacks the numbers (late publication, a field not carried across, or something else) is not shown here; it is a question for IP Australia (OQ7).

evidence.text: - **Restated with the register (U100, U101; ADR 0029).** The cause is publication: IP Australia's register holds an ABN, or an ACN that has one, for most of the marks IP RAPID leaves without. With it, 92.3% of Australian organisations' trade marks have a filer's ABN in FY2024, 91.4% in FY2025 and 90.9% in FY2026 (a fall of 1.4 points, against 24.2 by IP RAPID's alone: much reduced, not removed), and firms with a first observed linked trade mark number 14,728, 15,818 and 19,730 (4.3% to 7.0% of them already linked to IP another way, U101). Standard patents are not filled (U99), so their fall from 88.7% to 83.9% stands.

evidence.text:
- **Falls:** in 2009, standard patents fell 10.9% (26,598 to 23,707), designs 15.2% (6,060 to 5,136) and trade marks 4.5% (59,271 to 56,612), the year after the global financial crisis began; in 2022, trade marks fell 11.2% from the 2021 peak (88,751 to 78,844).

evidence.title: U25: Growth in standard patents has slowed to 0.4% a year; trade marks and designs are growing faster
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Standard patent applications grew 3.9% a year in the 1990s, 1.3% from 2000 to 2010, 2.0% from 2010 to 2019 and 0.4% from 2019 to 2025, with overseas applicants setting the pace. Trade marks grew 4.3% a year and designs 5.5% a year from 2019 to 2025.

- Australians' standard patents grew 1.1%, 2.5%, 0.9% and 0.9% a year in the four periods (by the filer's origin); overseas applicants' 4.2%, 1.1%, 2.1% and 0.3%.
- Trade marks grew 6.9%, 3.3%, 2.7% and 4.3% a year in the four periods, so their growth since 2019 is faster than in the 2010s but slower than in the 1990s.
- Designs grew almost entirely from overseas; Australians' ran at 1,903 (2022) to 2,678 (2013) a year from 1990.
- **Falls.** In 2009, standard patents fell 10.9% (26,598 to 23,707), designs 15.2% and trade marks 4.5%, the year after the global financial crisis began; trade marks fell 11.2% in 2022 from the 2021 peak.

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the IP rights lens)
evidence.text:
**For this observation**

1. Every trade mark and design was read from IP Australia's register through its APIs on 27 October 2026.
   - _Why:_ A sample can check accuracy, but filling gaps needs every record, so that every year is filled alike.
2. A filled value keeps IP RAPID's and takes the register's only where IP RAPID has none.
   - _Why:_ IP RAPID stays the base, and its own values can always be compared with the filled ones.

**Repairs made to the IP rights lens before any observation**

1. Where a right's applicants have no country recorded, its origin is "unknown", not "overseas".
   - _Why:_ Counting the unknowns as overseas had added 517,145 old patents to the overseas side.
2. Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
   - _Why:_ They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Things the analysis has found but cannot yet explain. They are kept in view, not explained away. Several are closed or narrowed: IP RAPID's innovation patents in 2016 (U67), by the review against IP Australia; the trade mark expedite fall of November 2018 (U34), by IP Australia's own register (U103); most of the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (B11), by a gap in older records (B55); and about half of the recent fall in first patent filers, by the name match (M12).

- Australians' direct filing of standard patents rose to 28.3% in FY2026 (U90), and provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed up less often, mostly by new and heavy individual filers (B38, M35); both could be priority claims recorded late (OQ18).
- The share of divisional applications about doubled among both Australian and overseas organisations, within the same filers (B15, M26); why is not in the data.
- Firms with a first observed patent fell from 1,167 (FY2021) to 810 (FY2024); innovation patents closed in August 2021 (U45). About half of the later fall is linking (M12).

evidence.title: U28: Around some policy changes filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses; around others nothing stands out
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Pauses when an Act began:** no trade mark registrations in January 1996 (Trade Marks Act 1995; 4,021 in March) and 113 patent grants in June 1991 (Patents Act 1990), against about 1,025 a month.
- **Nothing stands out:** joining the PCT (entries through it come about 30 months after filing abroad), the plain packaging of tobacco, and the 2018 and 2019 Productivity Commission responses. Overseas trade marks fell 17.2% in the year after Australia joined the Madrid Protocol (July 2001), but they had been falling since early 2000.
- **Against the direction expected:** after the designs grace period (March 2022), Australians' design applications fell 16.5% and overseas applicants' rose 0.2%. A grace period would not be expected to lower filing, so the fall has some other cause, which this comparison cannot name.
- All compare the 12 months after with the 12 before; trends and seasons are not allowed for here (B37 does).

pool.text:
With no agent recorded before the first renewal, 31.7% of Australians' trade marks filed FY2010 to FY2015 were in force after 10 years, against 50.8% with an attorney. evidence.title: U44: A few firms file most of the patents that firms file
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Of the 23,971 firms that filed standard patents, the top 1% filed 55.3% of them, while the typical (median) firm filed just one. Trade marks are less concentrated: the top 1% of filing firms filed 25.7%.

- **Standard patents.** 23,971 firms filed 183,989; the median firm filed 1 and the 90th percentile firm 7.
- **Trade marks.** 301,249 firms filed 1,018,160; median 1, 90th percentile 6; the top 1% filed 25.7%.
- **Designs.** 14,113 firms filed 77,794, and the top 1% filed 35.6%. Provisional applications: the top 1% of 24,905 firms filed 32.0%. Second-tier patents: the top 1% of 6,077 firms filed 12.2%.
- **What firms hold now.** 260,292 firms hold 1,262,125 rights; 116,240 hold 430,305 rights still in force, and the top 1% of those hold 28.7%.

evidence.title: U5: Standard patent applications held steady over the last ten years, while trade marks and designs rose
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
In FY2017 to FY2026 there were 28,798 to 32,960 standard patent applications a year. Trade marks rose from 72,652 (FY2017) to 98,189 (FY2026), designs from 7,727 to 10,388, and plant breeder's rights fell from 413 to 255. Second-tier patents peaked at 7,150 in FY2021, the year innovation patents closed, then fell to 52 (FY2026).

- Provisional applications ran at 4,143 to 5,343 a year in FY2017 to FY2025, then doubled to 10,069 in FY2026 (U8).
- In the chart, standard patents of "origin unknown" give way to "overseas" ones between about 1975 and 1990; from FY1990 at most 0.45% a year are of unknown origin (FY1993). The change is in what the register records, not necessarily in who filed.
- **Corrected.** Before 1983 for trade marks, 1986 for designs and September 1985 for provisional applications, the register holds only the rights still alive when it was computerised, so those early counts understate filings (U23).

- **Concentration:** 70 of 130 institutions filed a standard patent; CSIRO 481, UNSW 196, Monash 185, Sydney 156, Queensland 150 (the top 5, 47.4%; the top 10, 63.4%).
- **Filing with others:** 16.63% of CSIRO's standard patents have another founding applicant, Sydney's 42.95% and South Australia's 43.40%; across the lens 24.3% to 34.2% by five-year period. pool.title: B34: Across OECD members patenting rises with business R&D almost one for one, but changes in R&D barely go with changes in patenting
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Across 36 members, residents' patents per person rise with business R&D (rank correlation 0.853; a slope of 1.151 on log scales). Australia filed 103.3 applications per million people in 2016 to 2020, about what its R&D predicts (98.46). But across members the change in patenting over the decade goes with the change in business R&D at only 0.165.

- In 2006 to 2010 Australia filed 125 against 226.3 predicted (55.22%). The prediction intervals are wide (17 to 580), so Australia is within the members' range in both periods: its change in position came from falling R&D, not rising patenting.
- 23 members' residents filed less over the decade. Australia's patenting fell from 125 to 103.3 per million (about 17%) as its business R&D fell by 0.34 points of GDP.
- **So** the strong link is between countries' levels, which share a long history; within a decade the changes were not seen to move together (0.165 over 34 members).

events.answer:
**Universities’ patenting is concentrated in a few institutions, and research-intensive universities tend to file more patents per research work—not just more patents overall. But the latest analysis finds that size, research citations, patent-cited research and grant success overlap heavily, so they should not be treated as separate explanations.** That is the main reading of U84 (descriptive), B45 and Stage 3’s M23 (both observational). [1]

## How much do universities patent?

**U84 (descriptive)** found that research institutions collectively account for a small but growing share of standard patent applications filed from Australia: 4.80% in 1990 to 1994 and 8.96% in 2020 to 2024. Those figures cover research institutions generally, not universities alone. [2]

Among universities, U84 records these standard patent filing counts for 2017 to 2026:
- University of New South Wales (UNSW): 196. [3]
- Monash: 185. [4]
- Sydney: 156. [4]
- Queensland: 150. [4]

U84 also found that universities in its table filed between 1.29 provisional applications per standard application at Griffith and 2.58 at Sydney. [5]

## What goes with more university patenting?

**B45 (Stage 2, observational)** found that larger universities, universities whose research was more often cited by US patents, and those with more research grants per work tended to file more patents per work. [6] These are comparisons between universities: B45’s much weaker link between changes in research output and changes in patenting does not establish that growing a university’s research output will raise its patenting rate. [7]

**M23 (Stage 3, observational)** tested those measures together. Its main finding is that they largely reflect a shared pattern of research intensity: none had a separately detectable association with patents per work in both periods once the others were held together. [8]

More specifically:
- The share of research works cited by patents remained linked with patenting in 2010 to 2016, but the link was not detected once the other measures were held together in 2017 to 2023. [9]
- Size retained a link only in the later period. [9]
- Research citations per work and research grants per work had no detectable separate link in either period once the measures were held together. [10]

There is an important distinction here: **M38 (Stage 3, observational)** looked across universities, medical research institutes and other institutions together, rather than universities alone. In that broader group, research cited by patents remained associated with the institution’s own standard and provisional patenting after institution type, size, research citations and health-research grants were held together, in both periods. [11]

Holding factors together helps separate overlapping patterns, but it is not an experiment and cannot establish cause and effect.

## What about collaboration?

**U84 (descriptive)** found substantial differences in joint filing: 42.95% of Sydney’s standard patents and 43.40% of South Australia’s had another founding applicant. [12]

However, **B45 (observational)** did not detect an association between the share of grants involving industry partners and the share of patents filed jointly. The estimates were uncertain enough that a moderate link remains possible—this is not evidence that industry collaboration has no relationship with patenting. [13]

## Important counting and interpretation limits

- **Commercialisation companies matter.** U81 (descriptive) found that UNSW filed 96.5% of its applications through NewSouth Innovations; excluding that company would leave only 3.5% of its patents in the count. The completeness of the institution-and-company list remains an open question. [14]
- **Place-based counts can miss university patents.** U87 (descriptive) found that 50.34% of universities’ standard applications with a filer’s postcode in FY2017 to FY2026 used a real postcode with no residents, rather than a residential postal area. [15]
- **Patent citations are not proof of research use or public benefit.** U85 (descriptive) examines US patent citations only; citations may be added by an examiner or attorney and do not establish where Australian research is used. [16]

Taken together, the evidence points to patenting as one aspect of research-intensive universities, rather than a clearly separable result of any single research measure. [8] These remain exploratory findings: Stage 3’s first pass awaits the research owner’s review, and the atlas has not yet answered its broader questions about public value or who benefits.

events.answer:
**Universities’ patenting is concentrated, closely linked with their broader research activity, and easy to undercount. But the atlas does not establish that more research funding causes more patents—or that patent citations show where research is used.** These are a reading of descriptive findings U81 and U84 and observational findings M23 and B46. [1]

## How much do universities patent?

**U84 (descriptive)** places universities within a wider research-institution sector that accounts for a minority—but a rising share—of Australian patenting: research institutions filed 4.80% of standard patents filed from Australia in 1990 to 1994 and 8.96% in 2020 to 2024. Those are figures for all research institutions, not universities alone. [2]

Patenting is concentrated in a few institutions. In 2017 to 2026, the leading research-institution filers were CSIRO with 481 standard patents, UNSW with 196, Monash with 185, Sydney with 156 and Queensland with 150; together, the top five accounted for 47.4%. [3]

Universities also differ in how they file. U84 reports 1.29 provisional applications per standard application at Griffith and 2.58 at Sydney. [4]

## What goes together with university patenting?

**B45 (observational)** found that larger universities, universities whose research receives more citations, and universities with more grant success tend to file more patents per research work—not simply more patents overall. [5]

**Stage 3’s M23 (observational) substantially qualifies that picture:** when size, citations, research cited by patents and grant success are held together, none has a separately detectable association with patenting in both periods; the measures largely overlap as indicators of research intensity. [6]

More specifically, research cited by patents retained its association in 2010 to 2016, but it was not detected once the other factors were held together in 2017 to 2023; size retained its association only in the later period. [7] In everyday terms, it is difficult to separate these overlapping characteristics and say which one independently explains the differences between universities.

There is a useful contrast with **M38 (observational)**, which examined universities alongside medical research institutes and other institutions: the association between research cited by patents and institutions’ own patenting held in both periods after institution kind, size and other research measures were held together. [8] M38 deliberately covers a broader group than the universities-only M23, so the findings answer different comparisons. [9]

These remain associations, not evidence that changing any one characteristic would cause more patenting.

## What about collaboration?

**U84 (descriptive)** shows substantial differences in joint filing: 42.95% of Sydney’s standard patents and 43.40% of South Australia’s had another founding applicant. [10]

But **B45 (observational)** did not detect an association between the share of grants with industry partners and the share of patents filed jointly. Its uncertainty ranges still allow a moderate link, so this is not evidence that no relationship exists. [11] Nor is it a test of whether industry partnerships are associated with more patent applications overall: joint filing is a different outcome. [12]

## Important counting and interpretation limits

- **Include commercialisation companies.** U81 (descriptive) found that UNSW files 96.5% of its patent applications through NewSouth Innovations; without that company, only 3.5% of its patents would appear in the university’s count. The completeness of the institution-and-company list remains an open question. [13]
- **Place-based counts can miss university patents.** U87 (descriptive) found that, in FY2017 to FY2026, 50.34% of universities’ standard patent applications with a filer’s postcode carried a real postcode with no residents, outside the postal-area geography used in the analysis. [14]
- **Patent citations are not proof of research use.** U85 (descriptive) examines citations from US patents only; citations may be added by examiners or attorneys, and newer research has had less time to accumulate them. They do not establish where Australian research is used. [15]

Taken together, the evidence points to university patenting as part of a broader pattern of research intensity—not a simple league table of research performance or a demonstrated causal chain from grants to patents. [16]

- **Australians, above all individuals, often file without an attorney.** Overseas filers use an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents, Australian filers for 85.4%, and Australian individuals file 62.4% of their trade marks alone. Observations: U20, U48.
- **Provisional applications doubled in FY2026.** 10,069 against 4,143 to 5,047 a year before, mostly from individuals but from organisations too, both broadly and through a few heavy filers. It is in the filings, not the recording. Why is a question for IP Australia. Observations: U8.
- **Around some policy changes, filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses.** Rushes to file before a rule changed (Raising the Bar, 4.41 times Australians' usual month; the innovation patent's closure, 4.31 times), steps, and pauses when new Acts began; around other changes nothing stands out. These timings are the raw material for the natural experiments the later questions need. Observations: U28, U3.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Filing without an attorney still goes with far fewer grants.** With the route, year, state and co-filers held together, Australian individuals' patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often (35.8 raw), in both decades; trade marks and designs with no agent before the first renewal are less often in force after it. Not a cause: an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney. Observations: M1, M2.
- **Australian organisations' patents: three readings that still disagree.** At the same reach they are less likely to end (hazard ratios 0.648 to 0.811), yet they reach fewer offices and are cited about 27% to 30% less at the same reach, field, route and year. None of the three is value; they must be read together. Observations: M3, M4.

evidence.text:
- **Filing without an attorney goes with poorer outcomes.** Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 percentage points less often, in both decades and among examined applications too. evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Take Stage 2's comparison (filed alone against with an attorney) as the raw figure.
2. Fit one model of the yes or no outcome (granted or not) with the route, filing year, state and co-filers held together, and report the difference as an average difference in points.
3. Compare the held figure with the raw one, and give the outcome by Stage 3's rule (holds if at least half remains and the interval is clear of zero).
4. Repeat in the earlier decade, among applications with a field (holding the field), and among examined applications.

**Which gives observation M1:** Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often than those filed with an attorney once the route, filing year, state and co-filers are held together (FY2010 to FY2019), against 35.8 points with nothing held: 87.2% of Stage 2's gap remains, and 86.2% in the earlier decade. Trade marks filed alone show the same gap for individuals and organisations alike, almost untouched by what is held.

evidence.text:
Of the standard patents Australian individuals filed alone in FY2010 to FY2019, 4.8% were granted, against 40.6% of those filed with an attorney: a gap of 35.8 points (interval 33.9 to 37.5). In FY2000 to FY2009 the gap was 36.8 points. It stays among applications whose examination was requested (34.4 points).

- **Filing alone goes with not asking for examination:** 25.2% of individuals' lone applications were examined, against 75.9% with an attorney.

evidence.text:
With no agent recorded before the first renewal, 31.7% of Australians' trade marks filed FY2010 to FY2015 were in force after 10 years, against 50.8% with an attorney. With the filer's type, class, state, route and cohort held together the gap is 14.4 points, 75.5% of the raw 19.1; within individuals and within organisations it holds more fully. Designs show the same at their five-year renewal, almost untouched by what is held.

- **Within each type of filer** the gap holds more fully (85.3% to 94.6% left): individuals -11.8 and -12.0 points, organisations -15.1 and -10.8. Part of the pooled gap is who files alone: individuals, whose marks are less often in force either way (22.3% and 35.6% in FY2010 to FY2015).

section: How this moves the research forward
evidence.text:
Stage 1 answers none of the five questions. This is how the observation prepares the ground for them.

- **Q2. Who benefits, and who is underserved?** Filing without professional help is a possible sign of a barrier, or of a choice; individuals stand out.
- **Q4. Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?** If filing alone goes with worse outcomes (B6), help for those who file alone is one option IP Australia could weigh; whether it would change outcomes is not tested here.

_Linking an observation to a question is the analyst's guide to where it may help. It is not a finding._

Stage 2 answers none of the five questions either: it finds which measures go together. This is how the association prepares the ground for them.

- **Q1. What public value does the IP system create?** Lifetimes, reach and citations, the value signals, are tied to who files and in what field, so they must be compared within those groups.
- **Q2. Who benefits, and who is underserved?** Representation and origin go with outcomes, a first sign of who is served well and who is not.
- **Q4. Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?** Filing without an attorney goes with withdrawal, which is where help to file could matter.

section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (5 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Look for dates that cannot be true (before the register began, or a computer's default date).
2. Compare trade marks' registration dates with their filing dates before 1986.
3. Compare the "technology area" with the class for every type of right.

**Which gives observation U2:** Profiling found five quirks: a false end date (1 January 1970) on 1,282 rights; one trade mark registered before the register began; 121,207 old trade marks "registered" on the day they were filed; a "technology area" that only repeated the class for trade marks and designs; and an attorney flag that counted applicants as their own attorneys. Each was repaired.

section: IP Australia's conclusions and what the evidence adds
pool.text:
What IP Australia concludes, how strongly it says it, and what the evidence here adds (C1 to C12 from the first review; C13 to C16 from the second). None of IP Australia's conclusions is adopted here: that is the research owner's decision.

- **C1: The rise in provisional applications reflects digital tools, including AI, lowering the cost of a first filing.** Strength: "Consistent with"; "an important focus for ongoing analysis". Adds: U8: the rise is broad (single-filing individuals 1,538 to 2,507) and concentrated (54 individuals filed 1,528). Both fit; neither proves it. Since then, FY2025's fall in provisionals followed up within 12 months (6.66%, against 12.24% to 14.15% in FY2022 to FY2024) is in new and heavy individual filers (B38, M35).
- **C2: A firm's first patent or trade mark coincides with lasting gains in income and productivity.** Strength: "Dynamic associations, not definitive causal effects." Adds: Nothing to test. Stage 1 has no data on firms' performance.

pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Of 17,627 active R&D Tax Incentive claimants placed in a postal area, 48.3% have no IP filing linked to their business number, and 44.7% have no link to IP of any kind. Neither shows that a claimant never filed. There are 5.6 claimants per 1,000 businesses in major cities, 2.4 in inner regional, 1.8 in outer regional, 1.3 in remote and 0.6 in very remote areas.

- Claimants in outer regional and remote areas more often have no filing linked (57% and 56.5%, against 48% in the cities); inner regional areas are close to the cities (49.4%), and very remote areas hold only 11 claimants.

- **Why "no filing linked" is not "never filed".** A firm can file without its business number being recorded, or under a related company.
- These are counts by registered address, often a head office, not necessarily where the R&D is done.

events.answer:
**Filing without an attorney is linked with poorer outcomes, especially for Australian individuals’ patents—and most of that gap remains when the analysis holds other recorded factors together. But it does not show that using an attorney causes a better outcome.** That is the central finding of Stage 3’s M1 and M2, both observational findings. [1]

### Who files without an attorney?
Stage 2’s **B5 (observational)** found that Australian individuals were much more likely to file standard patents without an attorney or agent: **26.11%** of their filings in **FY2010 to FY2019**, compared with **3.54%** for Australian organisations, **1.14%** for overseas individuals and **0.28%** for overseas organisations. [2]

### Patents: a large grant gap that survives further testing
Stage 2’s **B6 (observational)** found that, for Australian individuals’ standard patents filed in **FY2010 to FY2019**:
- **4.8%** of those filed alone were granted, compared with **40.6%** filed with an attorney—a gap of **35.8 points**. [3]
- Only **25.2%** of applications filed alone had examination requested, compared with **75.9%** filed with an attorney. [4]

The grant gap was not just about whether applicants requested examination: B6 still found a gap of **34.4 points** among applications whose examination was requested. [5]

Stage 3’s **M1 (observational)** then held the filing route, filing year, state and co-filers together. For **FY2010 to FY2019**, the gap remained **31.2 points**, compared with **35.8 points** before those factors were held together; **87.2%** of the original gap remained. [6] In everyday terms, comparing applications on those recorded characteristics did little to explain away the difference.

M1 classified the link as **“holds”** for individuals in both decades. It was not universal across applicant groups: for Australian organisations in **FY2000 to FY2009**, M1 did not detect a difference either way. [7]

### Trade marks and designs: a similar link with staying in force
Stage 3’s **M2 (observational)** found that **31.7%** of Australians’ trade marks filed in **FY2010 to FY2015** with no agent recorded before the first renewal were still in force after **10 years**, compared with **50.8%** with an attorney. [8] Holding the filer’s type, class, state, route and cohort together reduced the gap from **19.1 points** to **14.4 points**, but most remained. [9]

M2 also found that designs with no agent before their first renewal were less often in force afterwards, with most of the gap remaining when the recorded factors were held together. [10]

### What can—and can’t—we conclude?
**The association is persistent, but it is not evidence of an attorney’s causal effect.** M1 cannot account for the filer’s resources, experience or the merit of the invention, and an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney—so the relationship can also run backwards. [11]

Taken together, M1 and M2 suggest that representation is an important marker of different outcomes, not proof that providing an attorney would close those gaps. [12] The atlas also leaves open whether filing alone reflects a barrier to professional help or a deliberate choice. [13]

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For inventors of international applications, the share estimated to be women is 14.6% for Australia, against WIPO's published 13.8%. But the median country is 4.5 points too high, and China (34.6% against 23.4%) and Korea (37.0% against 15.7%) far too high. So estimates are read for inventors in Australia only.

- The Netherlands, Spain, New Zealand, Finland and Ireland are within 2 points.
- The United States 20.0% against 15.3%; Germany 16.6% against 10.7%; Japan 16.3% against 9.0%.

- **Decision.** Estimates are read as levels for inventors in Australia only; for other countries only within one country over time; for China and Korea not at all.

events.answer:
The atlas points to **a low estimated share of women among inventors, substantial differences between technology fields, and a more qualified picture of differences between organisation and individual applicants**. These are estimates from names—not records of anyone’s gender—and the strongest interpretation is for inventors in Australia. [1]

## How many inventors are estimated to be women?

**U98 (descriptive)** examined inventors in Australia named on standard patents filed **FY2017 to FY2026**. The estimated shares of women were:

- **14.33%** on patents filed by Australian organisations. [2]
- **12.42%** on patents filed by Australian individuals. [2]
- **12.75%** on patents filed from overseas. These are still inventors in Australia, not overseas inventors. [2]

For provisional applications, **U107 (descriptive)** found estimated shares of **21.24%** for Australian organisations and **15.58%** for Australian individuals in **FY2017 to FY2026**. But this is **not a like-for-like comparison with standard patents**: provisional inventors are assigned the applicant’s country rather than their own. [3]

## Technology field makes a substantial difference

**B17 (observational)** found that women’s estimated share among inventors in Australia on standard patents varied widely by field in **FY2010 to FY2019**:

- Civil engineering: **4.2%**. [4]
- Transport: **5.2%**. [4]
- Pharmaceuticals: **24.4%**. [4]
- Biotechnology: **26.9%**. [4]

The ordering of fields was broadly consistent between **FY2000 to FY2009** and **FY2010 to FY2019**, with a rank correlation of **0.86**—meaning fields with relatively higher or lower shares tended to stay in similar positions. [5]

## Do organisations have more women inventors than individual applicants?

**For standard patents, the apparent advantage does not survive accounting for technology field.** Stage 3’s **M7 (observational)** found that, in **FY2010 to FY2019**, Australian organisations’ inventors had an estimated women’s share of **12.18%**, against **11.13%** for Australian individuals. The raw difference was not statistically detected; with field held together, the difference was **-2.82 points**, with organisations’ share lower. [6]

In plain English, comparing applicants across different mixes of technology can give a different impression from comparing them within the same field.

**For provisionals, the organisation–individual difference does hold under the factors tested.** **B18 (observational)** found shares of **21.19%** for Australian organisations and **16.12%** for Australian individuals in **FY2013 to FY2022**. **M7 (observational)** then found a difference of **+5.56 points** with year, state and co-filers held together, and found that the gap also held in the earlier decade. [7]

That result has an important limit: **technology field could not be held for provisionals because none has a field recorded in the dataset used**. [8] Holding measured factors together helps separate their associations, but it is not an experiment and does not establish a cause.

## How much confidence should we put in this?

- **These are name-based estimates.** U98 and U107 explicitly describe expected counts, not observed gender identities. [9]
- **The estimates are not equally reliable across countries.** U97 (descriptive) limits interpretation of levels to inventors in Australia and excludes interpretation for China and Korea because of problems with the name-based estimates. [10]
- **Coverage is uneven.** U95 (descriptive) identifies missing inventor countries for most patents filed only in Australia; the atlas’s limits page notes that countries are known mostly for patents also filed abroad. [11]
- **This is evidence about inventors, not all women participating in the IP system.** The atlas cannot estimate the gender of individual applicants because their identities are pseudonymised. [12]

Taken together, my reading is that **technology field is central to understanding women’s estimated representation**, while the organisation–individual comparison depends on the patent type and which other factors can be examined. These are exploratory observational patterns, not evidence that a field or applicant type causes the differences. [13]

evidence.title: B34: Across OECD members patenting rises with business R&D almost one for one, but changes in R&D barely go with changes in patenting
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Across 36 members, residents' patents per person rise with business R&D (rank correlation 0.853; a slope of 1.151 on log scales). Australia filed 103.3 applications per million people in 2016 to 2020, about what its R&D predicts (98.46). But across members the change in patenting over the decade goes with the change in business R&D at only 0.165.

- In 2006 to 2010 Australia filed 125 against 226.3 predicted (55.22%). The prediction intervals are wide (17 to 580), so Australia is within the members' range in both periods: its change in position came from falling R&D, not rising patenting.
- 23 members' residents filed less over the decade. Australia's patenting fell from 125 to 103.3 per million (about 17%) as its business R&D fell by 0.34 points of GDP.
- **So** the strong link is between countries' levels, which share a long history; within a decade the changes were not seen to move together (0.165 over 34 members).

The prediction intervals are wide, so Australia is within the members' range in both periods: its change in position came from falling R&D (B33), not rising patenting.
- **The changes:** across 34 members, the change in patenting from 2006-2010 to 2016-2020 goes with the change in business R&D at a Spearman rho of only 0.165; 23 members' residents filed less. Australia's patenting fell (a change of -0.083 in base-10 logs, from 125 to 103.3 per million, about 17%) as its business R&D fell by 0.34 points of GDP.
- **So** the strong link is between countries' levels, which share a long history; within a decade the changes were not seen to move together (rho 0.165 over 34 members). A lead for Q4: across members, a decade's change in business R&D has gone with little change in patenting; whether raising R&D would raise patenting is not something these data can show.
